Ignoring RTO/RPO when siting and designing, because business continuity belongs only to application owners
Spending the same capital on every closet regardless of impact, service dependency, or the cost of an outage
explanation: Facility investment should match the impact of losing the served service, including redundancy and operating discipline; slogans, ignoring recovery objectives, and equal spending on every closet discard that business context.
stem: Aligning facility investment with business criticality means:

choices: Cooling never contributes to outages, because electrical and network systems remain independent of thermal conditions
Only cyber attacks cause facility downtime, while physical plant failures are merely application symptoms
Utility, equipment, human, and environmental events all contribute; the dominant cause varies by site
Only utility events ever matter, because equipment, people, and environmental conditions cannot create facility downtime
explanation: Availability failures can arise from utility, equipment, people, cooling, and environmental conditions, with the mix varying by site; treating only cyber, utility, or cooling as universal misses the actual causal spread.
stem: Which statement about causes of unavailability is most balanced?

choices: Guaranteed lower energy cost forever, even when maintenance ownership and operational boundaries are left undefined
Elimination of all physical security needs because an IT-only organization has no facility-facing responsibilities
Faster automatic compliance with all building codes, because facilities and operations do not need to participate in change decisions
Gaps in change control, maintenance ownership, and incident response across trades
explanation: Reliable facilities require clear ownership across IT, facilities, security, and vendors; leaving maintenance, change control, and incident response at an IT-only boundary creates gaps rather than eliminating physical risk.
stem: Treating the data centre as only an IT department concern (with no facilities/ops partnership) risks:

choices: Recite the three buckets and treat the largest published percentage as law, even when the source does not support a stable share
Cooling can contribute a fixed one-third share, so start at the chiller for this site
Human error is the unverifiable majority, so train harder and stop investigating power, cooling, and site-specific evidence
Power path often leads facility events; cooling can cascade; human and process factors contribute — do not invent a fixed pie
explanation: The three-bucket cartoon is retired. Look at the path first; treat cooling as a cascade; treat people as contributing. Cite surveys as surveys. Refuse a fake percentage.
stem: A slide still lists power, cooling, and human error as three equal root-cause buckets and asks you to memorize this year’s survey share. The taught 2026 reading is:

choices: GPU colo is just retail colo with more kW; the rest are Tier names with no separate market or facility meaning
Four new names for retail colo cages, with no meaningful distinction in ownership, density, energization, or operating model
All four are Uptime plaques that describe a rating level rather than a product, ownership model, or energization path
Neocloud rents GPU capacity; GPU colo offers dense colocation; AI factory is owner-operated; BTM is an energization path
explanation: 2026 types are speakable nouns, not replacements for enterprise/colo/hyperscale. Neocloud is a business; GPU colo is still colo; AI factory is a plant; BTM is how watts arrive.
stem: A neocloud, a GPU colo, an AI factory, and a behind-the-meter campus walk into an oral. Kept beside the six classic types, the taught distinctions are:

choices: Pin the scope, planned-work treatment, measurement clock, and the fact that 99.99% is about 52.6 minutes per year
The Tier plaque on the wall — four nines is Tier III, so service scope and the measurement clock need no further review
Convert 99.99% into 52.6 minutes and stop, because a percentage has the same meaning per service, site, and component
Whether they used the 9 hours / 1 hour memory aid, without checking the service boundary or whose clock produced the number
explanation: A nines number without scope is marketing. Pin per-what, planned vs unplanned, and whose clock. Lead with 52.6 minutes, not the slogan, and do not crosswalk nines onto a plaque.
stem: A vendor says “we are 99.99%.” What do you pin before you treat the number as a claim?

choices: Enough for the same minutes of thermal inertia a 5–10 kW hall had, because rack density does not change the thermal clock
A cooling plan, because batteries reject heat and therefore replace the plant design for a dense rack
Not a cooling plan: thermal ride-through collapses toward seconds, with inlet or cold-plate conditions setting the clock
Proof the hall can skip Module 09 if the UPS sticker says 10 minutes, regardless of rack density or cooling response
explanation: Watts in the silicon are not heat rejected. Density collapses the window from minutes to seconds. This file only makes the availability point; the plant is Module 09.
stem: At 40–100 kW/rack, a UPS that holds the IT load after cooling stops is:

choices: Declare the hall white space and close the ticket, because a green UPS display proves the checkout service has no facility dependency
Name the accountable seat and demarc for the path, not just the green object; two green screens can still hide an ownership split
Treat dual PSUs as proof of dual utility, even when both supplies share a breaker, path, or upstream source
Recite a survey percentage and buy a bigger generator, without identifying the failed service boundary or who can restore it
explanation: Two green dashboards are not one owned path. Name the seats, name the demarc, then trace. Module 15 owns the 2.1 org heading; this item only makes you ask who owns the breaker.
stem: Facilities’ UPS screen is green and IT’s dual PSUs are lit, but checkout is down. In a colo the same sentence is “I thought they owned that breaker.” The first organizational move is:

choices: N+1 on the plaque means the window is free, so redundancy removes the need for a freeze or a path-trace review
Temporary N-0: work on the spare while the primary path is degraded; freeze or re-plan the change
Dual server PSUs make the window N-0-proof, because endpoint power supplies eliminate shared upstream maintenance risk
This is a cooling cascade, so start at the chiller even though the scenario concerns concurrent work on an electrical path
explanation: Redundancy enables maintenance; it does not survive working the last path. Call the window N-0. Do not steal Module 06’s path grammar — this is the mission concept only.
stem: Path A is already degraded. A tech opens Path B for “redundant” work in the same window. The mission-level diagnosis is:

choices: Both terms are deprecated because the industry standardized on AI factory as the only valid label for high-density computing
Neocloud is an official TIA-942 classification added for AI workloads, so the label is a standards designation rather than a market term
GPU colo is a formal Uptime Institute tier for facilities exceeding 50 kW per rack, with the rack threshold defining the rating
They are market terms for high-density AI facilities, not formal standards or rating systems
explanation: Neocloud, GPU colo, and AI factory are market vocabulary describing high-density, GPU-heavy facilities built for AI/ML workloads. They appear in IEA reports, industry press, and job postings but are not formal classifications in TIA-942, Uptime Institute tiers, or ISO standards. Interview fluency requires recognizing these terms as descriptive market language, not confusing them with rated or certified classifications.
stem: A job posting asks for 'neocloud and GPU-colo experience.' The correct framing is:

choices: Codes are adopted and enforced by an AHJ; many standards are voluntary unless referenced into code
Codes never address electrical safety
Standards always supersede local law
Codes are always free PDF white papers
explanation: The code is enforceable when adopted by the AHJ, while a standard is normally voluntary until code, contract, or policy references it; a white paper or free document is not automatically law.
stem: In CDCP awareness language, a “code” is best distinguished from a “standard” by:

choices: The Authority Having Jurisdiction enforcing the adopted code
The equipment vendor’s blog
Whoever emailed last
The marketing brochure
explanation: The AHJ’s adopted code controls the legal outcome when it conflicts with voluntary guidance; an email, blog, or brochure cannot displace that jurisdictional requirement.
stem: When a voluntary industry standard conflicts with the adopted electrical or fire code, who prevails?

choices: Separate frameworks with distinct criteria, processes, and owners—do not mix labels casually
Interchangeable brand names for the same certificate
Identical to ISO 9001 quality registration
Both issued exclusively by ASHRAE
explanation: TIA-942 Rated and Uptime Tier have distinct criteria, processes, and owners; they are not interchangeable brand names, ISO 9001 registrations, or ASHRAE certificates.
stem: TIA-942 “Rated” language and Uptime Institute “Tier” language should be treated as:

choices: Only network patch-panel colour
Topology/concurrency of facility infrastructure resilience (not a guarantee of zero human error)
Application software coding style
Only lighting lux levels
explanation: Uptime Tier concepts focus on facility-infrastructure topology and concurrent maintainability; patch-panel colour, application code, and lighting lux do not establish that resilience property.
stem: A careful statement about Uptime Institute Tier concepts is that they primarily address:

choices: A series addressing data centre facilities and infrastructures at an international standards level
A U.S.-only fire code article
A single Uptime certificate number
A diesel fuel chemical formula
explanation: ISO/IEC 22237 is an international series for data-centre facilities and infrastructure; it is not a Uptime certificate, a national fire-code article, or a fuel formula.
stem: ISO/IEC 22237 is best described for CDCP awareness as:

choices: An exclusive generator OEM manual
A European series of data centre design/operation related standards
A replacement for all local building permits
A North American only telecom cabling colour chart
explanation: EN 50600 is a European data-centre facilities and infrastructure series; it is not an OEM manual, a permit replacement, or a North American wiring colour chart.
stem: EN 50600 is best described for CDCP awareness as:

choices: Because international and regional series may both appear in RFPs, audits, or local practice even if not identical
Because their clauses use identical wording across editions
Because an AHJ may reject standards outside its adopted code
Because neither ever relates to facilities
explanation: International and regional series can both appear in RFPs, audits, and local practice without identical wording; tracking both is useful, while treating them as clones or as irrelevant misses the project context.
stem: Why might a multi-national operator track both ISO/IEC 22237 and EN 50600 awareness?

choices: Forbid any use of IEC documents
Adopt, adapt, or publish national documents that may reference or align with international work
Regulate cafeteria menus rather than technical facilities
National bodies can automatically void international standards
explanation: National standards bodies may adopt, adapt, or reference international work, with alignment varying by country and topic; they do not forbid IEC use, regulate cafeteria menus, or automatically void international documents.
stem: National standards bodies often:

choices: The facility standard alone specifies every device model
They only apply to residential kitchens
They replace the need for an AHJ
Facility performance depends on equipment and systems that are themselves covered by product/system standards
explanation: Product and system standards define performance for devices such as cabling, fire detection, and electrical equipment that feed the facility outcome; the facility standard cannot name every model, replace the AHJ, or limit the topic to kitchens.
stem: Sub-component standards (e.g., for cabling, fire detection devices, or electrical equipment) matter because:

choices: One global document covers every jurisdiction and product
Only blog posts are authoritative
Only PUE marketing scores are required
A mix of codes, facility series (TIA/ISO/EN), product standards, and owner specs—with AHJ as the legal floor
explanation: The practitioner maps codes, facility series, product standards, and owner specifications under the AHJ’s legal floor; one global document, a blog, or a PUE score cannot cover every jurisdiction and product.
stem: Which is the most accurate “landscape” view of data-centre guidance?

choices: ISO issues Tier badges
Slide decks always include formal Uptime certification
Tier is a defined Uptime framework/process; casual “equivalent” claims confuse stakeholders and audits
Equivalence is automatically granted by TIA
explanation: Uptime Tier terminology names a defined framework and process, so an informal “equivalent” claim can create false assurance; ISO, TIA, and a slide deck do not automatically award that certification.
stem: Claiming a site is “Tier III equivalent” based only on a vendor slide deck is risky because:

choices: A telecommunications industry facility standard framework with rating language of its own
The same thing as an Uptime Institute Tier certificate by default
Something that may appear in design specifications
Related to data centre infrastructure topics
explanation: TIA-942 Rated is its own telecommunications-facility framework, not an Uptime Tier certificate by default; it can still appear in specifications and address related infrastructure topics without becoming the other program.
stem: TIA-942 Rated concepts should not be described as:

choices: Legal codes plus any standards the project or jurisdiction incorporates must be identified and followed
Only the cheapest standard applies, because a project may ignore adopted code, referenced standards, and the AHJ once a low-cost option is found
AHJ review is optional forever
Standards never need listing
explanation: The project must identify adopted codes and every standard incorporated by jurisdiction or contract; the cheapest document, optional AHJ review, or an unlisted reference cannot define compliance.
stem: A design specification that says “comply with applicable codes and referenced standards” implies:

choices: Practitioners must check which document is adopted or specified in that jurisdiction and project
Only U.S. documents exist
National always means weaker, so a practitioner can select the international document without checking adoption, jurisdiction, or project specification
International always voids local law
explanation: The governing document is the one adopted or specified for the jurisdiction and project; national is not automatically weaker, and an international series cannot void local law by prestige.
stem: Which statement about international vs national standards is most careful?

choices: Recognize an international facility/infrastructure series exists alongside other frameworks
Memorize every normative clause number without context, because awareness of the series and its relationship to codes has no practical value
Replace electrical code inspections
Ignore EN 50600 entirely always
explanation: Awareness lets learners recognize ISO/IEC 22237’s place among facility and infrastructure frameworks without memorizing every clause; it does not replace electrical inspections or justify ignoring EN 50600.
stem: ISO/IEC 22237 awareness for CDCP learners mainly helps them:

choices: Designing only residential lighting
Selecting office chair ergonomics exclusively
Projects, suppliers, or customers in Europe reference the EN data centre series
Working only with purely North American code questions and no EU touchpoints, suppliers, customers, or project documents referencing European practice
explanation: EN 50600 matters when European projects, suppliers, or customers reference that regional series; residential lighting, office ergonomics, and a purely North American project without an EU touchpoint do not create that trigger.
stem: EN 50600 awareness is especially relevant when:

choices: Only internal runbooks, because product safety, listing, and AHJ acceptance do not affect electrical equipment used in a facility
Hot-aisle poster guidelines only
Product safety standards and AHJ/listing requirements—not from a facilities “tier” label alone
PUE contests
explanation: Equipment marking follows product-safety standards and AHJ or listing requirements; an internal poster, a PUE contest, or a facility Tier label does not provide product acceptance.
stem: Product listing/marking expectations for electrical equipment typically come from:

choices: Assume both are enforced as law everywhere
Treat both as identical to ISO 27001
Always pick the one with the higher Roman numeral in marketing, because a larger label proves stronger topology, process, and contractual meaning
Compare criteria, assessment process, and contractual meaning—then use the framework the owner actually requires
explanation: The owner should compare each framework’s criteria, assessment process, and contractual meaning before selecting the required one; law, ISO 27001 branding, and a larger marketing numeral are not substitutes for that comparison.
stem: Which is a responsible comparison of TIA-942 and Uptime approaches?

choices: Always override the AHJ
Are illegal to read
Offer recommended practice that becomes binding only if adopted by code, contract, or policy
Carry criminal penalties by themselves in all cities, even when the document has not been adopted by code, contract, or organizational policy
explanation: The guideline recommends practice and becomes binding only through code, contract, or policy adoption; it does not automatically override the AHJ or carry criminal penalties by itself.
stem: Guidelines and best-practice documents differ from codes in that they usually:

choices: IP address planning
Generator fuel chemistry exclusively
Only the brand of coffee in the NOC, because device listing, installation, and performance are unrelated to the facility fire strategy
Device performance, listing, and installation expectations feeding the facility fire strategy
explanation: The fire-detection device standard shapes device performance, listing, and installation within the facility fire strategy; it does not set IP planning, generator chemistry, or unrelated office choices.
stem: A sub-component standard for fire detection devices would most likely influence:

choices: Preferred by a project AHJ as code
A naming and contractual mismatch that can fail bid evaluation or audit expectations
ISO 22237 can require the Uptime/TIA substitution
Accepted as identical under the bid's terminology, despite different assessment meanings
explanation: An RFP’s Uptime Tier certification requirement is not met by an unagreed TIA Rated design-intent phrase; the frameworks, assessment meanings, and bid obligations differ.
stem: If an RFP requires “Uptime Tier III certification,” substituting “TIA Rated-3 design intent” without agreement is:

choices: Architects ignore inspectors, because an adopted code and voluntary preference have equal legal force once the design team chooses a framework
Only international standards matter
Standards bodies fine the AHJ
Where adopted code and voluntary preferences diverge, enforcement authority of the AHJ controls the legal outcome
explanation: “AHJ wins” means the enforcing authority applies adopted code when voluntary preferences diverge; international documents and standards bodies do not replace that local legal decision.
stem: The phrase “AHJ wins” in CDCP study shorthand means:

choices: Both only apply to residential attics
Neither ever appears in data centre RFPs
EN 50600 → only U.S. NEC article; ISO 22237 → only diesel ASTM grade, so neither series belongs in a data-centre standards discussion
EN 50600 → commonly European context; ISO/IEC 22237 → international series awareness
explanation: EN 50600 is associated with European data-centre practice, while ISO/IEC 22237 is the international facilities series; neither is a residential rule, a U.S. NEC article, or a fuel grade.
stem: Which pair correctly associates series awareness with region/context (at a high level)?

choices: Decorative appendices rather than contractual requirements
Project documents typically replace building permits because they remove jurisdictional approvals
Contractual requirements that may exceed code minimums but cannot lawfully undercut adopted code
Irrelevant when an ISO number is mentioned because the international series replaces local project controls
explanation: Owner specifications are contractual requirements that may exceed code minimums but cannot undercut adopted code; they are not decorative, permits, or irrelevant once an ISO number appears.
stem: Owner’s project specifications sit in the standards landscape as:

choices: Communicate requirements precisely and avoid false equivalence between frameworks
Ignore local inspectors
Eliminate the need for engineers, because naming a standard is enough to resolve design, code, and contractual decisions
Memorize clause numbers for trivia, rather than communicate which framework, requirement, and assessment path actually applies
explanation: Standards literacy lets a team name the applicable framework and requirement precisely; it does not replace engineers, local inspectors, or the reasoning needed to apply a clause.
stem: A key reason CDCP emphasizes standards literacy is to:

choices: Keep TIA Rated and Uptime Tier labels distinct, because their criteria, owners, and assessment processes are not interchangeable
State which framework and assessment path the owner actually requires, after confirming the contract and jurisdictional context
Map design features to the chosen framework’s concepts carefully
Invent a hybrid “Tier-Rated-5” label to impress auditors without defined criteria
explanation: The made-up hybrid label has no defined criteria or assessment meaning; keeping TIA and Uptime labels distinct, naming the owner-required process, and mapping features to that framework avoids false assurance.
stem: Which is NOT a sound practice when citing facility resilience frameworks?

choices: International standards typically replace every national electrical code automatically, so adoption and local interpretation no longer matter
Ban national standards bodies, because international technical documents cannot coexist with national adoption or reference practices
Apply to marketing material rather than technical design
Provide broadly usable technical documents that countries and markets may adopt or reference differently
explanation: International standards provide broadly usable technical alignment that countries and projects may adopt or reference differently; they do not replace national codes, ban standards bodies, or turn marketing into design criteria.
stem: International standards development typically aims to:

choices: AHJ organizational charts
Uptime Tier certificates, because a site-level rating defines the performance and listing of every cabling and firestop product
Sub-component / product-system standards and listings supporting the facility
ISO 22237 entire-series replacements, because a facility series makes product listings and component categories unnecessary
explanation: Cabling categories and firestop listings are product or system requirements that support facility performance; they are not an AHJ chart, a site Tier certificate, or a replacement for the ISO facility series.
stem: Cabling performance categories and firestop product listings are examples of:

choices: Copy a blog’s PUE number into the permit set
Assume no requirements exist for life safety, because an unlisted data-centre topic cannot affect the AHJ's adopted fire and electrical obligations
Ignore all voluntary standards, because code silence means an owner cannot adopt good engineering practice or referenced guidance
Apply owner-approved voluntary standards and good engineering practice while still meeting all code minimums that do apply
explanation: When code is silent on a data-centre-specific issue, owner-approved voluntary standards and good engineering practice can guide design while applicable code still controls; a blog number, blanket code silence, or refusal to use guidance is not a professional method.
stem: If local code is silent on a data-centre-specific topic, a common professional approach is to:

choices: TIA, ISO/IEC 22237, and EN 50600 are among the named series learners should not conflate with Uptime Tier branding
EN 50600 is a type of UPS battery, because the series name describes equipment chemistry rather than facility guidance
Only one series exists worldwide, so TIA, ISO/IEC 22237, EN 50600, and Uptime terminology can be treated as one document
ISO 22237 is a lux meter brand
explanation: TIA, ISO/IEC 22237, and EN 50600 are distinct facility-oriented series that learners should map without equating them to Uptime Tier branding; they are not a battery, a single worldwide document, or a lux-meter brand.
stem: Which statement best reflects CDCP-level awareness of multiple facility series?

choices: Operators may ignore both if PUE is low
The marketing brochure wins
Any international standard automatically voids national law
The AHJ-enforced code requirements prevail for compliance
explanation: The AHJ-enforced adopted code governs legal compliance; a low PUE, marketing brochure, or international standard cannot void that jurisdictional requirement.
stem: When a voluntary data centre standard conflicts with a legally adopted building or electrical code, the governing principle is:

choices: Irrelevant to any design conversation, because topology, assessment, and contractual meaning do not depend on the framework named
Only about cabling colors
Identical trademark-free synonyms usable interchangeably in contracts without care, because the labels carry the same criteria and assessment process
Related resilience concepts that must not be mixed as if they were the same certification scheme
explanation: TIA Rated and Uptime Tier both discuss resilience but remain distinct programs with different terminology and assessment; calling them synonyms or ignoring the framework makes the design and contract claim ambiguous.
stem: TIA-942 “Rated” language versus Uptime Institute “Tier” language should be treated as:

choices: It only covers office lighting aesthetics, because the series has no relationship to data-centre facilities or infrastructure
It is a proprietary single-vendor product manual
It is a multi-part international framework addressing data centre facilities and infrastructures
It replaces every national electrical code worldwide, so local adoption, AHJ enforcement, and project specifications no longer matter
explanation: ISO/IEC 22237 is a multi-part international framework for data-centre facilities and infrastructure; it is not a vendor manual, an office-lighting document, or a replacement for national code.
stem: ISO/IEC 22237 series awareness for CDCP-level study mainly means recognizing that:

choices: An appliance energy label for home refrigerators
A European framework of data-centre facilities and infrastructure standards
A battery chemistry formula manual for UPS vendors
A North American residential wiring code
explanation: EN 50600 provides a European framework for data-centre facilities and infrastructure review; it is not a home-appliance label, battery formula, or North American residential wiring code.
stem: During a facilities review, a project team uses EN 50600 references. What does the series provide?

choices: National documents are archival and do not affect local construction choices
Local codes, climate, grid practice, and AHJ interpretation still govern what may be built and operated
International documents are less detailed than local project requirements, making local sources the primary references
Vendors typically write national rules instead of standards bodies
explanation: International guidance can inform design, but local codes, climate, grid practice, and AHJ interpretation govern what may be built and operated; national documents are not archival and vendor preference is not law.
stem: International standards versus national/local requirements often create tension because:

choices: They replace the need for any system-level design, because listed components make facility integration, coordination, and protection unnecessary
They only apply to furniture, so cabling, firestop, and equipment safety marks do not affect facility assemblies
They forbid all redundant paths
They help ensure assemblies and products meet defined performance/safety criteria used in the facility
explanation: Sub-component standards help products and assemblies meet defined safety and performance criteria used by the facility; listed parts do not eliminate system coordination, furniture is not the scope, and they do not forbid redundancy.
stem: Sub-component standards (e.g., cabling performance, firestop listings, equipment safety marks) matter because:

choices: Tier labels never influence buyer risk perception, contractual interpretation, or the assurance communicated by a sales document
Self-assessment always equals formal certification, because a site's own checklist has the same program controls and assurance as an independent award
Uptime Tier terminology implies a defined program; misuse creates false assurance
Standards forbid writing the word tier in any language
explanation: Uptime Tier terminology implies a defined program, so an informal self-assessment can create false assurance and contract risk; it is not meaningless, self-certifying, or forbidden vocabulary.
stem: Using “Tier III” casually in a sales document when only an informal self-assessment was done is problematic mainly because:

choices: Are illegal to cite in design briefs, so owners cannot use a voluntary guideline through contract or policy
Guidelines can automatically supersede AHJ rulings, because recommended practice has higher authority than an adopted local requirement
Provide recommended practice that may be adopted or referenced but are not law by themselves
Carry criminal penalties when a voluntary guideline is cited
explanation: The guideline supplies recommended practice that may be adopted or referenced but is not law by itself; it cannot supersede an AHJ or acquire criminal penalties merely by being cited.
stem: Guidelines (non-mandatory best-practice documents) differ from adopted codes in that guidelines:

choices: Assume one brochure covers power, cooling, fire, and security completely, so no framework or AHJ boundary needs to be checked
Know major families (TIA/Uptime naming, ISO/IEC 22237, EN 50600, codes) and when each applies
Ignore all documents outside one country, because TIA, ISO/IEC 22237, EN 50600, and local codes cannot coexist in one project
Memorize every clause number of every series before day one on site, rather than recognize which family applies to the question
explanation: CDCP awareness means recognizing when codes, TIA/Uptime terminology, ISO/IEC 22237, or EN 50600 applies; one brochure, one country’s documents, or memorizing every clause is not the operational skill.
stem: A practical CDCP takeaway on the standards landscape is to:

choices: Whether average rack density exceeds an arbitrary marketing number, because density determines code compliance without jurisdictional review
Whether the logo wall looks modern, because appearance is a sufficient proxy for adopted code compliance and AHJ acceptance
Whether any international standard PDF is on a shelf, because possession of a document proves the site's legal requirements are met
Whether applicable adopted codes and AHJ requirements for the jurisdiction have been met
explanation: The code-compliance answer depends on the applicable adopted codes and AHJ requirements for that jurisdiction; a density number, modern logo wall, or stored international PDF cannot prove compliance.
stem: If an insurer or customer questionnaire asks whether the site is “code compliant,” the honest answer depends on:

choices: Keep Availability Class, TIA Rated, and Uptime Tier distinct; there is no Class 3 = Rated-3 = Tier III conversion
Protection Class is the converter between Rated and Tier, because protection and topology are one rating lattice
Class 3 is TIA’s new name for Uptime Tier III after the 942-C rename, so the newer label makes the frameworks equivalent
Finish the conversion: Availability Class is the official translator that makes Rated-3 equal Tier III, so the labels can be swapped in the contract
explanation: Rated lives in TIA-942-C, Tier in Uptime, Availability Class in EN 50600 / ISO/IEC 22237. The numbers rhyme on purpose; collapsing them is the trap.
stem: An RFP writes “Class 3 / Rated-3 / Tier III equivalent” as one bullet. The taught reading is:

choices: EN 50600 is a fire code that overrides the local AHJ, so its facility requirements replace adopted jurisdictional law
EN 50600 is Uptime’s third plaque and does not need a number, because the European series is merely branding for a certification
EN 50600 is the European data-centre facilities series alongside ISO/IEC 22237; it carries Availability Class and separate Protection Classes
EN 50600 is informal flavour text; only 22237 is a real series, so European projects need not identify the document
explanation: Write the number. EN 50600 is the European twin of 22237, not a vibe and not a fire code. Availability Class and Protection Classes live in that family as separate axes.
stem: A designer says ISO/IEC 22237 is already on the shelf, so EN 50600 is just “European lineage” with no number to learn. The correction is:

choices: Whether Uptime also issued an Availability Class sticker for the same hall, because the plaque names are interchangeable evidence
None — TCCD is the single sticker that covers drawings, the building, and operations forever, so no constructed or operational evidence is needed
TCCF and TCOS remain open: a design review is not the constructed plant or its operational practice
Whether PUE is below 1.3, which converts TCCD into constructed-facility proof and establishes operational sustainability automatically
explanation: Uptime issues three certificates — TCCD, TCCF, TCOS — not one plaque. Paper can be right while the built plant or the operating regime is not.
stem: A colo brochure says “Tier III facility” and produces only a TCCD letter. What question is still open?

choices: Convert the TIA numeral to 99.982% and call the conversion the pin, rather than identify the edition and framework
Replace TIA language with Availability Class 3, which is the 2024 rename and makes the contract's framework unambiguous
Pin ANSI/TIA-942-C (2024) and ask which edition is open; do not call TIA Rated language Tier
Accept it — TIA-942-C still says Tier, so the old wording is current law and no edition check is needed
explanation: Cite ANSI/TIA-942-C (2024) unless the contract names an older edition. The Rated-not-Tier rename is the point of pinning C; an un-yeared citation is soft.
stem: Someone says “TIA Tier III” while pointing at an un-yeared “per TIA-942” clause. The edition-years rule asks you to:

choices: Memorize 99.671 / 99.741 / 99.982 / 99.995 as the current topology standard, because the table is still the governing Uptime definition
Uptime Tier describes topology, not a guaranteed availability percentage; do not replace the withdrawn table with a new crosswalk
Replace 99.982 with a newer blog percentage so the nines-to-Tier crosswalk stays current, even though the source withdrew the prediction table
True for TCOS but not for TCCD — swap the percentage onto the operations plaque, because topology and availability are the same claim
explanation: The cargo-cult nines table is withdrawn. This course will not hand you a replacement percentage. Ask for the path and which plaque, not a nine.
stem: A slide recites “Tier III means 99.982% availability” (and the I–IV downtime table). The taught response is:

choices: Accept both — a nameplate plus a KPI is the classification; no further evidence is needed because equipment labels and ratios prove topology
Ask for the one-line and applicable Uptime plaque; photos and PUE do not prove topology
Treat the nameplate photo as TCCF and the dashboard as TCOS, because a component and a meter establish the three plaques
Convert the PUE into 99.982% and treat that as the missing Class/Tier crosswalk, without checking the path or assessment program
explanation: A one-line diagram is evidence of a topology claim. A nameplate, a PUE, or a nine is not. Ask which plaque (TCCD / TCCF / TCOS) and do not collapse Class into Tier.
stem: A vendor “proves” the hall is Availability Class 3 / Tier III by emailing a UPS nameplate photo and a PUE dashboard. The diagnostic move is:

choices: Treat the PUE dashboard as TCOS and the WUE plot as TCCF, because efficiency ratios prove both construction and operations
PUE, WUE, and CUE are KPI ratios, not topology classes; ask for the one-line
Convert the PUE into 99.982% so the KPI becomes the missing Class/Tier crosswalk, rather than identify the facility path
Accept the annex — a good PUE is concurrent maintainability, and 1.2 is the law because a KPI determines topology and rating
explanation: ISO/IEC 30134 is the KPI series. PUE / WUE / CUE are meters, not a topology class. A good PUE does not make a hall concurrently maintainable. WUE depth is Module 10. No nines-to-Tier crosswalk. No invented PUE target.
stem: An RFP annex lists “PUE / WUE / CUE” under “topology class” and treats a 1.2 PUE as Rated-3. The taught reading is:

choices: ERF and ERE are different metrics; do not collapse the letters
ERF is the 2024 rename of Availability Class; ERE is the TIA Rated letter, so energy reuse terminology maps to facility ratings
Either letter converts to a single PUE target that is now law, regardless of the metric's definition or boundary
Agree: Energy Reuse Factor and Energy Reuse Effectiveness are one KPI with two spellings, so the source and denominator need not be checked
explanation: 30134-6 is ERF (Energy Reuse Factor). ERE is not that part. The series has more than three letters; this course names the distinction and stops. No single PUE target as law. Sustainability-track depth is not this leftover.
stem: A slide writes “ERF = ERE” and files both as the same ISO/IEC 30134 letter. The correction is:

choices: Swap B for Availability Class 3 — that is the 2024 rename of TIA, so the standards can be treated as one lattice
Pin ANSI/TIA-942-C (2024); the 2017 B set is an older edition unless the contract still cites B
Convert the B numeral into 99.982% and treat the conversion as the edition, rather than name the document and publication year
Accept B: later editions did not replace it, so 2017 is still the Rated document and no edition pin is needed
explanation: Cite ANSI/TIA-942-C (2024) unless the contract names an older edition. B is superseded as the current Rated document. This is not a nines table and not a Class/Tier crosswalk.
stem: Procurement hands you a 2017 TIA-942-B drawing set and says it is current Rated-3 under today’s edition. The edition-pin is:

choices: TCOS requires prior TCCF; the three plaques are sequential, not parallel
Swap the missing TCCF for 99.982% so Operational Sustainability can stand alone, because a percentage substitutes for the prerequisite award
Accept: Design Documents, Constructed Facility, and Operational Sustainability are three parallel badges, so any one can stand alone without sequence
Treat the TCOS letter as TCCD, because the design-documents acronym determines the sequence without checking the program definitions
explanation: Uptime conditions TCOS on prior TCCF. Full names: Tier Certification of Design Documents, Constructed Facility, Operational Sustainability. Parallel-badge reading is the fail. Rated ≠ Tier ≠ Availability Class stays un-crossed. No replacement nine.
stem: A broker offers “Tier Certification of Operational Sustainability” as a stand-alone Gold badge, with no prior Constructed Facility award, and says the three plaques are interchangeable parallel stickers. The apply move is:

choices: Lobby artwork style
Proximity and independence of utility substations/feeds and right-of-way constraints
Colour of exterior cladding only
Number of conference rooms
explanation: Electrical diversity depends on independent substations or feeds plus rights-of-way that can reach the site; cladding, artwork, and conference-room count do not make two utility paths independent.
stem: Which site-selection factor most directly affects multi-path electrical utility diversity?

choices: Only aesthetic landscaping
Long-term operability of plant yards, fuel systems, and building envelopes under water events
Nothing if the site has a raised floor indoors
Only wireless signal strength
explanation: Flooding and storm surge can disable plant yards, fuel systems, switchgear, access, and the building envelope; an indoor raised floor cannot protect outdoor plant, and the risk is not merely landscaping or wireless signal.
stem: Flood plain and storm-surge exposure primarily threaten:

choices: They can replace the need for power redundancy
Application availability often depends on diverse external network paths as much as on hall design
They affect cafeteria Wi-Fi rather than carrier paths
Carriers use cafeteria Wi-Fi instead of physical entrance rooms
explanation: Diverse carriers and meet-me paths reduce correlated external network failure alongside power and cooling resilience; they do not replace power redundancy or describe cafeteria Wi-Fi.
stem: Why do fibre and carrier meet-me diversity matter in site selection?

choices: Only exterior signage fonts
Air distribution, cable pathways, and equipment clearances in white space
Diesel cetane rating
Badge printer toner choice
explanation: Floor-to-floor and clear height constrain air distribution, cable pathways, and equipment handling; diesel chemistry and badge-printer supplies do not determine that structural envelope.
stem: A facility criterion for floor-to-floor height / clear height is important mainly because it affects:

choices: Only the CEO office artwork
Only hot-aisle posters
Security/NOC spaces, loading/staging, generator/fuel yard, and utility intake areas
A single shared restroom with no other spaces
explanation: Supporting facilities include generator and fuel yards, loading or staging, utility intake, and security or NOC spaces; executive artwork, posters, and a lone restroom do not make a site operable.
stem: Supporting facilities that enable operations typically include:

choices: Furniture catalogues can determine seismic anchorage requirements
Nothing if dual UPS exists
Structural design, anchorage, and sometimes geographic site rejection
Paint shear strength determines structural site risk
explanation: Seismic and geotechnical risk drives structural design, equipment anchorage, and sometimes rejection of the parcel; furniture catalogues, paint strength, and dual UPS do not resolve ground motion.
stem: Seismic and structural site risks should influence:

choices: Quiet commercial campus with dual utility corridors
Multiple diverse fibre providers on campus
High external contamination, vibration, or explosion risk from neighbouring industrial hazards
Adequate truck turning radii
explanation: Industrial adjacency can introduce contamination, vibration, or explosion risk that requires mitigation or site rejection; diverse carriers, utility corridors, and truck access are positive site attributes rather than that hazard.
stem: Which environmental adjacency is often a site-selection red flag?

choices: Software license counts
DNS TTL values
Heavy IT, battery, and cooling equipment placement without structural reinforcement
Emergency light colour only
explanation: Slab loading limits where heavy IT, batteries, and cooling equipment can be installed without reinforcement; software licences, DNS settings, and light colour do not carry structural load.
stem: Slab loading capacity as a facility criterion primarily limits:

choices: Generators need indoor placement at this site
Yards typically store marketing banners rather than fuel equipment
AHJs prohibit generator installations at this site
Fuel storage, clearances, acoustics, and maintenance access require real estate that a tight urban parcel may lack
explanation: Generator yards need real estate for fuel storage, clearances, acoustics, and maintenance access; a tight urban parcel can therefore fail before equipment selection, and marketing storage or a blanket prohibition is not the criterion.
stem: Why is generator yard space a supporting-facility concern during site selection?

choices: UPS batteries require city water flow continuously
Servers drink municipal water directly
Cooling towers and some plants depend on reliable makeup water quantity and quality
Fibre optics need daily washing
explanation: Water-cooled plant needs reliable makeup-water quantity and quality; UPS batteries, fibre optics, and direct server consumption are not the cooling-tower site dependency.
stem: Water availability for cooling (where water-cooled plant is planned) is a site factor because:

choices: Security starts and ends at the rack door only
Fencing is always illegal
Site selection and layout should support controlled approach, vehicle management, and layered access
Cameras replace structural setbacks always
explanation: Site security needs controlled approach, vehicle management, and layered access from the campus inward; a rack-only lock, a blanket fence ban, or cameras alone cannot provide that perimeter strategy.
stem: Which statement about site security perimeter planning is most accurate?

choices: Improving change success rates
Increasing dual-utility diversity
Creating unsafe equipment moves, delayed installs, and blocked emergency paths during receiving
Raising ceiling clear height automatically
explanation: Weak loading and staging create unsafe moves, delayed installation, and blocked emergency routes; they do not improve change success, utility diversity, or clear height.
stem: Inadequate staging and loading docks most often hurt operations by:

choices: Only tax incentives for murals and public-facing finishes, with no relationship to climate, heat rejection, or outdoor design conditions
USB cable lengths
HVAC energy, plant type options, and outdoor design conditions for capacity
Badge colours
explanation: Climate and free-cooling potential shape HVAC energy, plant options, and outdoor design conditions; murals, USB lengths, and badge colours do not determine the cooling envelope.
stem: Climate and free-cooling potential influence site selection mainly through:

choices: Unlimited chiller capacity with no trade-offs, because roof and yard constraints do not limit plant placement or service access
Automatic dual utility feeds
Elimination of fire detection
Design compromises on cooling plant placement, capacity, or even site rejection
explanation: Limited roof or yard area can constrain cooling-plant placement, capacity, and maintenance access enough to reject the site; it cannot create unlimited chillers, utility feeds, or a fire-detection exemption.
stem: A building with limited roof/yard space for heat rejection may force:

choices: Hypervisor license SKU
CPU clock speed only, because human operations are determined by workload rather than NOC, security, storage, or maintenance space
Presence of suitable NOC, security, storage, and maintenance access spaces
BGP AS number
explanation: Human operations require suitable NOC, security, storage, and maintenance spaces; a hypervisor SKU, CPU speed, or BGP number describes IT rather than the staff environment.
stem: Which is a facility criterion related to human operations, not only equipment?

choices: It determines IP subnet size
Routers require daily physical commuting by packets, so transportation access has no bearing on fuel, equipment, or emergency response
Fuel, equipment deliveries, and emergency response depend on reliable road access
It sets lux levels
explanation: Road access supports fuel and equipment deliveries and emergency response; IP subnet size, packet travel, and lux levels are not transportation criteria.
stem: Transportation access matters for site selection primarily because:

choices: Diverse carriers and utilities are available
Floor loading is adequate, so deed restrictions and easements cannot constrain fuel, antenna rights, or other resilience infrastructure
Deed restrictions, easements, or landlord constraints block generator fuel or antenna rights needed for resilience
Security screening exists
explanation: The campus can have diverse carriers and adequate loading yet fail if easements, deed restrictions, or landlord rules block fuel or antenna rights; utility access alone does not remove those legal constraints.
stem: Shared multi-tenant campuses can still fail a “good site” test if:

choices: A clean RF environment can replace grounding systems, shielding, and equipment mitigation because it removes every electrical interference concern
A clean RF environment improves PUE
It may interfere with sensitive equipment and require mitigation or site rejection
RF environment affects cafeteria microwaves rather than sensitive equipment
explanation: Nearby high-power transmitters can interfere with sensitive equipment and require mitigation or site rejection; a clean RF environment does not replace grounding or improve PUE, and the concern is not cafeteria equipment.
stem: Electromagnetic or RF environment near high-power transmitters is a site concern because:

choices: Utility, network, hazards, climate, logistics, and legal rights—before interior finishes
Only carpet colour and logo walls
Only number of vending machines, because utility, network, hazard, climate, logistics, and legal-rights checks belong after the shortlist
Only social media check-ins
explanation: Early short-listing weighs utility and network rights, hazards, climate, logistics, and legal constraints before finishes; carpet, vending machines, and social-media activity do not establish site feasibility.
stem: Which combination best summarizes early site short-listing criteria?

choices: Documented MOPs, because procedures alone provide the secure, maintainable plant and staff space that supporting facilities require
Presence of dual power paths
Lack of secure, maintainable space for electrical and mechanical plant and ops staff
Adequate clear height
explanation: The facility is incomplete without secure, maintainable space for mechanical and electrical plant and operating staff; documented procedures and dual paths help but cannot substitute for the missing physical support envelope.
stem: A “supporting facility” gap that can undermine a well-designed white space is:

choices: Data centres never grow, so future power, cooling, and floor-plate options cannot affect the initial site decision or relocation risk
Expansion only needs software licenses
Power, cooling, and space upgrades have long lead times; growth without room forces costly relocation
AHJs forbid expansion always
explanation: Future land or floor-plate options preserve room for long-lead power, cooling, and space upgrades; software licences, a no-growth assumption, or an AHJ prohibition do not solve physical expansion.
stem: Future expansion land or floor plate options are site criteria because:

choices: Facility criteria (structure, utilities, envelopes, plant space) bound what IT architectures can reliably deploy
IT architecture can override building physics in this project
Software defines floor loading while building limits follow IT architecture
Network diagrams set flood elevations
explanation: Structure, utilities, envelopes, and plant space bound what IT can deploy reliably; software, network diagrams, and IT architecture cannot override floor loading or site physics.
stem: Which statement is most accurate about facility criteria vs pure IT architecture?

choices: Flooding can disable power, cooling, access, and life-safety systems for extended periods
Water can improve electrical insulation, so flood history has no bearing on recovery planning
Flood plains do not affect insurance under standard site policies
Raised floors make flooding irrelevant everywhere
explanation: Flood history can disable power, cooling, access, and life-safety systems together, extending recovery; water is not protective insulation, insurance is not automatically unaffected, and a raised floor is not universal flood control.
stem: Flood plain and historical flood data matter in site selection primarily because:

choices: Decorative fountains only, because utility proximity has no relationship to independent power paths or correlated utility risk
Independent power paths and reduced correlated utility risk where available
Lower ceiling heights
Elimination of all UPS systems by regulation
explanation: Independent utility paths reduce correlated power risk where available, but they do not lower ceiling height, remove UPS requirements, or turn proximity into a decorative feature.
stem: Proximity to high-quality dual utility feeds is a site criterion mainly to support:

choices: Only the color of exterior cladding, because structural loading, clearances, delivery paths, and service access do not constrain plant
Only the brand of lobby coffee
Only the number of visitor parking stickers
Structural loading, clearances, delivery paths, and service access for large equipment
explanation: Heavy plant needs structural capacity, clearances, delivery routes, and service access for installation and maintenance; cladding, coffee, and parking stickers do not carry or service that equipment.
stem: Which facility criterion most directly affects whether heavy power and cooling plant can be installed and maintained?

choices: They are optional aesthetics with no availability impact, because fuel, water, telecom entry, and perimeter controls do not support the IT load
IT racks alone determine site risk, so external campus systems are omitted from site selection and maintenance planning
Maintenance access is unnecessary
Critical IT availability can depend on these external and campus support systems remaining functional
explanation: Fuel, water, telecom entry, and security perimeter are supporting systems whose failure can remove IT availability; they are not optional landscaping, rack-only risk, or maintenance-free details.
stem: Supporting facilities (e.g., fuel storage, water, telecom points of entry, security perimeter) should be evaluated because:

choices: Ground motion and soil conditions influence structural design, equipment anchorage, and outage risk
Seismic zones never affect data centres, because structure, anchorage, and outage risk are independent of ground motion and soil conditions
Only network latency depends on soil type, so structural design and equipment anchorage need no geotechnical input
Geotech reports only serve landscaping
explanation: Ground motion and soil conditions affect structural design, equipment anchorage, and outage risk; seismic conditions are not irrelevant to data centres, limited to networking, or a landscaping-only concern.
stem: Seismic and geotechnical risk assessment for a candidate site is important because:

choices: Guaranteed free dark fibre, because transport corridors cannot affect contamination, vibration, pollution, or emergency access
Accident, vibration, pollution, and emergency-access interference risks
Automatic Tier certification, because nearby transport hazards are converted into a facility rating rather than a site risk
Zero electromagnetic environment
explanation: Airports, rail, and highways can introduce accident, vibration, pollution, and emergency-access interference; a nearby corridor does not guarantee fibre, a facility rating, or a clean electromagnetic environment.
stem: Airport flight paths, rail lines, and major highways near a site raise concerns about:

choices: Retrofits can have ample floor-to-floor height and plant space, so existing constraints do not affect design
Greenfield projects bypass life-safety, planning, and utility approvals
Neither needs life-safety systems
Existing buildings may constrain floor loading, slab-to-slab height, risers, and plant yard space
explanation: Existing buildings can constrain floor loading, slab-to-slab height, risers, and plant yards, making retrofit feasibility difficult; greenfield does not bypass approvals and neither approach removes life-safety obligations.
stem: When comparing a greenfield build to retrofitting an existing building, a key facility-criteria difference is often:

choices: Removing all need for on-site network design, because diverse carriers and entries make internal path planning unnecessary
Eliminating physical security, because a second telecom path prevents physical access and perimeter failures
Cooling the white space automatically
Reducing correlated communications failure risk for the campus
explanation: Multiple telecom paths and diverse Points of Entry reduce correlated communications failure into the campus; they do not remove internal network design, physical security, or cooling requirements.
stem: Multi-path fibre and diverse telecom Points of Entry support site selection goals by:

choices: Introduce contamination, explosion, or emergency-response risks that affect plant and staff
Only improve outdoor air quality, because industrial emissions cannot contaminate intakes or affect staff and plant safety
Only lower insurance premiums always, because neighboring hazards reduce rather than increase contamination, explosion, and response risk
Never affect cooling intake design
explanation: Industrial neighbours can introduce contamination, explosion, and emergency-response risks affecting plant and staff; they do not reliably improve air quality, lower insurance, or leave cooling intakes untouched.
stem: Industrial neighbor hazards (chemical plants, heavy manufacturing emissions) are site factors because they can:

choices: Generators never need fuel, so long-duration utility loss creates no space, access, or resupply requirement for on-site generation
Long-duration utility loss requires space, access, and resupply paths for on-site generation
Yards are only for employee barbecues, because generator placement and fuel logistics are unrelated to supporting-facility planning
Fuel logistics are purely a marketing concern
explanation: Long utility loss makes generator space, fuel storage, delivery access, and resupply paths part of supporting-facility design; a generator does need fuel, and the yard is not a marketing or barbecue area.
stem: Adequate generator yard and fuel logistics planning is part of supporting facilities because:

choices: Only interior paint selection, because temperature, humidity, snow, and wind do not affect envelope or outdoor plant survival
Automatic exemption from standards, because climate extremes remove rather than add requirements for cooling, envelopes, and equipment survival
Whether copper or fibre may be used indoors
Envelope, cooling plant sizing envelopes, and outdoor equipment survival requirements
explanation: Temperature, humidity, snow, and wind set envelope, cooling-plant sizing, and outdoor-equipment survival requirements; they are not only paint choices, code exemptions, or an indoor copper-versus-fibre decision.
stem: Climate extremes (temperature, humidity, snow load, wind) influence site and facility criteria mainly by driving:

choices: Automated sites with no on-site staff cannot be affected by roads or response distance
Emergency services do not interact with data centres, so road distance is irrelevant
Road access can affect cafeteria catering rather than recovery
Remote sites with poor access can lengthen recovery and complicate 24×7 operations
explanation: Remote sites with poor roads or distant services can lengthen recovery and complicate 24×7 staffing; automation does not make emergency response, catering, or road access irrelevant.
stem: Staffing and emergency response access (roads, distance to services) matter for site selection because:

choices: Insufficient expandable power, cooling, and white-space/plant real estate
Having too many spare conduits, because extra pathways consume growth space without helping future power, cooling, or white-space capacity
Documented spare capacity pathways, because planning for expansion creates a larger constraint than the physical power, cooling, or plant envelope
Modular expansion provisions
explanation: Expandable power, cooling, white-space, and plant real estate preserve growth; extra conduits and modular provisions help rather than limit it, while initial rack count alone is not the future constraint.
stem: A facility criterion that often limits future growth more than day-one IT load is:

choices: The facility uses only passive cooling with no outdoor plant ever, so water rights and discharge planning cannot affect the site decision
Evaporative or water-dependent heat rejection and fire water supplies are part of the design concept
IT load is zero, so water availability and wastewater rights remain irrelevant even if the proposed site includes water-dependent plant
The site is purely a dry storage warehouse with no IT
explanation: Evaporative or water-dependent heat rejection and fire-water supply make quantity, quality, and discharge rights first-class site criteria; passive cooling, zero IT, or a dry warehouse would not create that dependency.
stem: Water availability and wastewater discharge rights can be decisive site factors when:

choices: The dual-feed lead time is the go/no-go, so a quoted feeder schedule overrides queue position and study status
Pin queue position, studies, security, and a realistic energization date; feeder lead time is not the queue
A closed land deal and a poured slab prove the hall will energize on the quoted feeder week, even without utility studies or posted security
This year’s published gigawatt request-book total decides the site without a project-specific queue position, study, or security posting
explanation: The feeder lead-time quote does not prove energization; queue position, study phases, security, and a realistic date determine the interconnection path, not a generic request-book total or a signed slab.
stem: A utility slide says “power available” and a project plan quotes a dual-feed SKU lead time. What is the 2026 go/no-go for whether the hall ever energizes?

choices: Refuse the story: two laterals and a lead-time SKU do not prove energization
Treat two nameplates on one wall as proof the second independent feed will be studied, even without a queue position or posted security
Accept the pair of laterals as dual path; the remaining risk is only the quoted lead time, not queue position, studies, or security
Specify a larger UPS/ATS/generator string here
explanation: Two utility labels and a feeder lead-time SKU do not prove independent energization; the missing queue position, interconnection study, and financial security are the site decision, not a larger UPS or a wall of laterals.
stem: Sales: “Utility A and Utility B are on the building; dual-feed lead time is booked.” There is no queue position, no interconnection study, and no financial security. The diagnostic move is:

choices: BTM is a site type; walk away if land, fuel or gas, or permits cannot host the plant
A later generator add-on you specify in this module (ATS sequence, UPS ride-through, islanding)
Proof the site has no grid risk, so interconnect can be ignored even when the proposed plant needs export, backup, or black-start capability
Another name for two utility laterals landed on opposite corners of the hall
explanation: Behind-the-meter describes the site’s energization model, so the parcel must host land, fuel or gas, and permits; it is not a later ATS detail, proof of no grid risk, or a synonym for two utility laterals.
stem: A brochure labels the parcel a behind-the-meter / on-site generation campus. In this module that phrase is:

choices: Every BTM pitch is a walk; on-site generation is never a legitimate site type, regardless of land, fuel, permits, or operating model
Flood plus a raised floor is the missing control, so plant hosting, interconnect, and fuel or gas paths do not matter
You must first draw the Module 06 UPS/ATS/generator one-line before any site decision, rather than checking whether the site can host the plant
The site cannot host the plant, so BTM is not a credible energization story
explanation: Without land, fuel or gas, and permits the BTM plant cannot be hosted, and BTM does not mean immunity from grid or interconnection constraints; a raised floor and a UPS one-line do not cure that missing site path.
stem: The tour says “BTM campus — no grid risk.” There is no plant land, no fuel or gas path, and no emissions permit. Walk because:

choices: Recite the brochure type list; Module 03 owns the 2026 type nouns and the facility need not test power, water, fiber, or queue risk
Score power, water rights, fiber, and queue—not brochure type labels
A PUE dashboard plus a universal 250 psf floor statute, because metrics replace site-specific utility and water analysis
Dual-cord servers, which replace water rights and queue position because endpoint redundancy resolves every campus-level constraint
explanation: AI-campus site review must score power, water rights, fibre, and queue evidence; brochure labels, endpoint dual cords, and an invented floor statute or PUE target do not resolve campus constraints.
stem: An “AI factory / neocloud” deck offers GPU colo, dedicated hall, and AI campus as the site answer. The speakable criteria are:

choices: Score power, water rights, fiber, and queue; logos are not diversity
Last year’s published fiber-cut percentage, which you must memorize as law rather than walk the physical paths and confirm water or queue evidence
Siting footnotes only; two logos equal diverse OSP and marketing MW equals interconnected power, so no site evidence is needed
Indoor problems a raised floor converts into non-events, including flood and long fiber cuts, so external site constraints need no review
explanation: Marketing megawatts and carrier logos are not interconnection or path evidence, so water rights, physical OSP diversity, and queue position remain open; an invented outage percentage or raised floor does not close those site risks.
stem: A neocloud pitch quotes marketing megawatts and two carrier logos. Water rights are “TBD.” Nobody can name a queue position. Treat grid and fiber as:

choices: Accept the claim: once the queue and BTM arrangement are cleared, curtailment is only a utility-failure issue and needs no operating handoff
Reject the absolute claim; confirm category and hand curtailment actions to M15 EOP 4
Use the April 2026 interconnection request total as a universal curtailment frequency, instead of checking this site's category and operating agreement
Calculate UPS/ATS autonomy in M03; the site module owns the power-path response and no curtailment procedure is needed
explanation: The qualifying BTM arrangement can still carry category-specific curtailment, so reject an unrestricted-dispatch claim and hand the action to the operating procedure; a queue statistic or UPS sizing exercise does not define this site’s trigger.
stem: A site has completed its large-load interconnection path and uses a qualifying net-metering / behind-the-meter arrangement. The owner says, ‘That means unrestricted dispatch.’ What should the M03 site review catch?

choices: Record curtailment and hand the trigger and action sequence to M15 EOP 4
Treat the instruction as proof that the interconnection queue failed and discard the BTM site plan, without checking the agreement or operating category
Assume behind-the-meter islanding is automatic, so no load-reduction procedure or utility trigger needs to be documented
Quote the regional interconnection queue volume as the site's guaranteed curtailment exposure, instead of confirming the site's category and agreement
explanation: The site review records any agreement-specific curtailment trigger and hands the action sequence to M15 EOP 4; it does not treat curtailment as proof the queue failed, assume automatic islanding, or substitute regional queue volume for the site agreement.
stem: During a site review, a behind-the-meter campus is told it may need to reduce load under its qualifying ERCOT arrangement during tight conditions. What is the correct M03-to-M15 handoff?

choices: TIA-942 uses 'Rated' (Rated-1 through Rated-4), not 'Tier' — Tier is an Uptime Institute term
No defect — TIA-942 and Uptime Institute use the same Tier terminology interchangeably, with identical labels and assessment meanings
Minor defect — Tier III and Rated-3 are identical, so the label is functionally correct for both standards and needs no correction
No defect — TIA adopted Uptime's Tier terminology in the 942-B revision, making the two rating systems interchangeable
explanation: TIA-942-B §5.3 defines 'Rated-1' through 'Rated-4' for infrastructure rating levels. 'Tier I' through 'Tier IV' is Uptime Institute's terminology from their Tier Standard. The two systems have similar intent but different requirements and assessment processes. Calling a site 'TIA-942 Tier III' conflates two separate standards. A design consultant must distinguish Rated (TIA) from Tier (Uptime) and cite the correct standard for each claim.
stem: A vendor claims 'TIA-942 Tier III certified.' The terminology defect is:

choices: Incomplete — Rated-3 requires concurrent maintainability of the entire path, not just UPS redundancy
Valid — 2N UPS capacity is the sole requirement for Rated-3 classification, so the rest of the distribution and maintenance path need no assessment
Valid if the UPS units are from different manufacturers for supply-chain diversity, even when the complete critical path is not concurrently maintainable
Incomplete only if the cooling system is less than N+1 redundant, because Rated-3 does not require maintainability of other facility paths
explanation: TIA-942-B §5.3.4 defines Rated-3 as 'Concurrently Maintainable' — any single component in the power or cooling path can be removed for maintenance without interrupting IT load. 2N UPS capacity addresses one component but says nothing about distribution paths, transfer switches, cooling, or fire suppression. Rated-3 is a topology claim about the entire infrastructure, not a capacity claim about one subsystem.
stem: A design claims Rated-3 because it has 2N UPS capacity. According to TIA-942-B, the claim is:

choices: Pin the edition (942-B or 942-C) — requirements differ between editions and 'TIA-942' alone is ambiguous
No correction needed — TIA-942 editions are backward-compatible, so any edition satisfies the reference and the contract needs no edition pin
Default to the newest edition since older editions are automatically superseded on publication, even when the contract or design was prepared under an earlier edition
No correction needed — the assessor will select the appropriate edition during the audit, after the ambiguous contract has already shaped the assessment
explanation: TIA-942-B (2017) and TIA-942-C (2024) have different requirement sets — topology definitions, electrical criteria, and cabling standards evolved between editions. A contract that says only 'TIA-942 compliance' is ambiguous: the designer may build to 942-B while the owner expects 942-C. Edition pinning (e.g., 'TIA-942-B Rated-3') removes the ambiguity. Standards are not auto-superseded in contracts; each party may assume a different edition.
stem: A contract references 'TIA-942 compliance' without specifying an edition. The design-consultant correction is:

choices: No distinction — the phrase 'Designed to' is legally equivalent to 'Certified by TIA'
No distinction — TIA issues compliance certificates for every design that follows the standard
'Designed to' requires a registered TIA assessor signature before the claim can be published
'Designed to' is a self-declaration — it does not imply third-party assessment of compliance
explanation: TIA-942-B §1.2 defines requirements but does not mandate or provide an assessment program. 'Designed to TIA-942-B Rated-3' is a self-declaration by the designer or owner — it may or may not have been verified by a third party. A due-diligence reviewer should ask whether an independent assessor validated the claim and, if so, request the assessment report. Self-declaration and third-party assessment are distinct; the marketing phrase does not prove either.
stem: A marketing sheet says 'Designed to TIA-942-B Rated-3.' A due-diligence reviewer asks for the assessment report. The distinction is:

choices: Acceptable if the claim is consistent with what other staff members also assert verbally, because repeated statements substitute for records and observation
No defect — verbal confirmation from the facility manager is sufficient audit evidence, even without records, observations, or another verifiable statement
Acceptable if the auditor documents the verbal claim in the audit report as management attestation, because recording a claim converts it into objective evidence
A verbal claim is not audit evidence — evidence requires records, observations, or verifiable statements
explanation: ISO 19011:2018 §3.9 defines audit evidence as 'records, statements of fact or other information which are relevant to the audit criteria and verifiable.' A verbal claim ('we follow the schedule') is not verifiable on its own. The auditor must request the maintenance log, work orders, or other records that corroborate the claim. Accepting unverified assertions undermines the audit's objectivity.
stem: An internal auditor accepts 'we follow the maintenance schedule' as evidence of compliance. According to ISO 19011, the defect is:

choices: No finding — ad-hoc testing by experienced technicians is an acceptable alternative to documented procedures and controlled evidence
Minor nonconformity — tests are still being performed, so the gap is procedural rather than operational and does not affect demonstrated compliance
Observation only — procedural documentation is a recommendation, not a requirement under TIA-942, even when evidence depends on repeatable records
Major nonconformity — missing a required procedure is systemic and affects the site's ability to demonstrate compliance
explanation: ISO 19011:2018 §6.4.8 distinguishes major from minor nonconformities. A major nonconformity is systemic — it affects the organization's ability to meet requirements or indicates a breakdown in the management system. Missing a documented procedure entirely (not just a gap in one instance) is systemic: the site cannot demonstrate repeatable, auditable compliance. Minor nonconformities are isolated deviations from an otherwise functioning system.
stem: An audit finds that the site has no documented procedure for generator load-bank testing — tests are performed ad-hoc by individual technicians. The lead auditor classification is:

choices: Pin the edition after fieldwork so the report can reference the most favorable requirements, even though the applicable criteria should govern the fieldwork
No correction needed — the auditor selects the edition based on what the site can pass, rather than the requirements in force for the engagement
No correction needed — all TIA-942 editions have identical audit criteria, so an edition pin would add no usable information
Pin the edition before fieldwork — audit findings depend on which edition's requirements apply
explanation: ISO 19011:2018 §5.2 requires audit objectives and criteria to be defined before the audit begins. TIA-942-B and TIA-942-C have different requirement sets; an unpinned criterion leaves ambiguity about which requirements the auditor is checking. Selecting or switching editions mid-audit — or after fieldwork — compromises objectivity. The audit plan must state 'TIA-942-B Rated-3' or equivalent before the first site visit.
stem: An audit plan lists 'TIA-942 compliance' as the criterion without specifying an edition. The internal auditor correction is:

choices: Lead auditor — leads third-party certification audits for external clients and therefore is the required role for an organization's own internal review
Internal auditor — audits the organization's own systems to identify gaps before external assessment
Either role — internal and lead auditor are interchangeable titles for the same function, regardless of audit independence or reporting line
Neither role — self-audits are not recognized under ISO 19011 audit frameworks, so an organization cannot perform a preparatory audit
explanation: ISO 19011:2018 §7.2.3 distinguishes internal auditors (first-party audits of one's own organization) from lead auditors (who manage audit teams, typically for second- or third-party audits). An organization auditing itself for TIA-942 readiness uses internal auditors. Lead auditors manage external or certification audit teams. The roles are not seniority levels; they serve different audit contexts.
stem: An organization wants to conduct its own TIA-942 compliance audit without external assessors. The role that applies is:

choices: Queue position and study timeline are irrelevant because grid operators process all requests simultaneously, regardless of upgrade scope or project size
Acceptable if the site uses behind-the-meter generation, which bypasses every queue, study, and permitting process universally and guarantees energization without upgrades
Acceptable if the site has a signed PPA, since a PPA guarantees immediate interconnection without a completed study or transmission upgrade
The gap is critical: energization depends on queue position, study phases, and upgrade scope, not an unsupported availability claim
explanation: LBNL's 'Queued Up' reports document multi-year interconnection backlogs in U.S. grids. Queue position determines when studies begin; study phases (feasibility, system impact, facilities) each take months to years; identified upgrades add construction time. A site that shows 500 MW 'available' without queue position, study phase, or upgrade scope cannot commit to an energization date. PPAs do not guarantee interconnection; BTM does not universally bypass queue processes.
stem: An AI-campus site selection shows 500 MW available 'once the interconnection is complete' but does not state the queue position or study timeline. The review gap is:

choices: Store bulk diesel under every tile
Eliminate all need for grounding
Create a service space for airflow and/or cable distribution beneath the IT floor
Replace fire detection
explanation: An access floor creates service space for underfloor airflow and/or cable distribution; it is not bulk-fuel storage, a grounding substitute, or fire detection.
stem: Raised-access floors in data centres are commonly used to:

choices: Lux at the work plane
Only the weight of a single caster wheel
The load assumed spread over a large area of the floor system
