explanation: Monitoring is production infrastructure: it needs protected power, a network path that survives, and a maintenance regime, because going blind during an outage is precisely when it is needed. Leaving it unpowered during utility loss is the specific failure -- the monitoring dies at the moment its data becomes decisive.
stem: A best practice for auxiliary systems is to treat monitoring infrastructure as:

choices: Correlation always proves the network team is at fault
Cross-domain correlation speeds root-cause isolation when cooling plant and room environment interact
Systems should never share timestamps
It replaces mechanical expertise entirely
explanation: Cross-domain correlation speeds root-cause isolation when cooling plant and room environment interact; it does not prove one team is at fault, eliminate timestamps, or replace mechanical expertise.
stem: Correlating BMS alarms with EMS temperature spikes helps operators because:

choices: Complete silence from the alarm system in all conditions
Automatic root-cause analysis of the underlying condition
Chattering alarms and desensitisation
A higher mean time between failures for the plant
explanation: Poor threshold design creates chattering, alarm fatigue, and missed real events; it does not produce silence in every condition, automatic diagnosis, or better plant reliability.
stem: Thresholds set without hysteresis or seasonality awareness often cause:

choices: Recite RDHx / D2C / immersion families and the W-class plant so this file owns cooling hardware

CDU / secondary-loop leak at the skid, QDCs, hose trays and cold-plate/RDHx drip pans, plus loop flow / temperature / pressure on both sides of the isolation HX, plus seconds-scale inlet or cold-plate rate-of-rise — a hall rope is not that coverage; hardware families stay in Module 09
Treat ISO/IEC 22237 Availability Class as equal to TIA Rated or Uptime Tier so the rope can be skipped
Quote a leak percentage that proves a single hall zone is enough
explanation: This file owns the points, not the plant. Secondary loop is its own leak and telemetry domain. Hall rope is not CDU coverage. No invented leak percent. Availability Class stays in Module 02. Liquid families stay in Module 09.
stem: A 2026 interviewer asks which first-class points a liquid-cooled GPU row needs beyond the raised-floor CHW rope. The taught answer is:

choices: Approve: hall rope plus a 15-minute average plus a leak percent is the 2026 clock
Convert the packet into the Module 09 liquid-family oral so the points question goes away
Recite Availability Class plaques in this file so Module 02 does not have to

Reject the packet: a hall rope is not CDU-loop coverage and a 15-minute CRAC-return average is the wrong clock — page on seconds-scale inlet or cold-plate rate-of-rise and on loss of N+1 CDU, not the last unit; Availability Class is taught in Module 02 alongside TIA, not equal to Rated or Tier; liquid families stay in Module 09; isolate-the-loop EOP craft is Module 15; do not invent a leak percent
explanation: Analyze the collapse. Hall rope and a 15-minute average are the wrong coverage and the wrong clock. Page on rate-of-rise and on loss of CDU redundancy. Do not steal Module 02 Availability Class or Module 09 plant. EOP craft is Module 15. No invented leak percent.
stem: Reviewer is handed a GPU-row monitoring packet: “Raised-floor rope is green so the CDU loop is covered; trip on a 15-minute CRAC-return average; page only when the last CDU dies; Availability Class here equals Rated/Tier; write the isolate-the-loop EOP in this file; cite a leak percent so the AHJ will sign.” You should:

choices: Add rate-of-rise sensing
Wait for the absolute threshold and disregard the slope
Move the life-safety logic into the DCIM dashboard
Set one universal degrees-per-minute value for every row
explanation: NFPA 72 (2025) §3.3.70.10 recognizes rate-of-temperature rise alongside threshold detection. A fast rate-of-rise signal adds an early operational layer; waiting for the threshold misses the slope, moving life-safety logic into DCIM crosses a boundary, and one universal rate overclaims.
stem: A GPU-row thermal packet has only a fixed-temperature alarm; a fast inlet sensor shows a sharp rise in seconds. The best gap review is:

choices: Let EMS replace the FACU whenever its sample rate is faster
Keep the fast EMS page supplemental; preserve the listed FACU path
Disable fixed-temperature detection once EMS is commissioned
Publish one EMS threshold as the universal fire-code setting for every GPU row
explanation: NFPA 72 (2025) §§3.3.70.10 and 26.6.3.2.2.2 keep rate-of-temperature-rise detection and listed fire-alarm signaling in their proper boundaries. Faster EMS sampling does not replace the FACU, disabling threshold protection removes a safeguard, and one universal row threshold overclaims.
stem: An operator proposes: “Our EMS samples the GPU row every few seconds, so it can replace the listed fire-alarm control unit.” The correct boundary is:

choices: Rely on a technician's memory of the original rack layout
Change the utility entrance arrangement before tracing the physical path
Remove labels during the move so the new assignment can be decided later
Use consistent circuit, port, and asset labels tied to current records so the physical path can be traced
explanation: Consistent labels tied to current records let the operator trace the disputed power and network path after a move; memory, utility redesign, or removing labels does not resolve the physical identity question.
stem: After a rack move leaves a power circuit and network port disputed, which labelling practice most quickly supports troubleshooting?

choices: Treat the latest drawing as authoritative when field verification disagrees
Treat as-built accuracy as a presentation concern once construction photos exist
Wrong paths and isolation points mislead responders
Avoid version control so one informal copy can stay in circulation
explanation: Stale drawings create false confidence during emergencies and maintenance; field verification, controlled records, and version history remain necessary after construction photos exist.
stem: As-built documentation that diverges from reality is dangerous because:

choices: MTTR is unrelated to spare parts and procedures in facilities
Statistical reliability and maintainability concepts
Only software uses these terms
MTBF promises zero failures in that period for every asset
explanation: MTBF describes reliability and MTTR maintainability, together guiding design and process; spares and procedures still affect MTTR, and MTBF never promises zero failures.
stem: MTBF and MTTR are most useful when teams remember that:

choices: Define response and restore times, coverage, and escalation for the service
Prohibit all vendor contact with the equipment under the SLA
Allow unlimited scope without measurable service boundaries
Specify only the vendor logo color and marketing identity
explanation: The owner needs measurable response and restore times plus coverage and escalation for the critical service; prohibiting contact, removing boundaries, or specifying branding does not make the alarm response accountable.
stem: A vendor SLA says “best effort,” but a critical cooling alarm requires a timed response. Which clause should the owner require before signing?

choices: Use compressed air toward the intakes so dust leaves the work area quickly
Use a particulate-controlled method that protects equipment and electrical systems
Skip cleaning under raised floors even when contamination is documented
Wet mop the PDU interior with an unverified chemical to capture the debris
explanation: The supervisor should require a particulate-controlled method that protects equipment and electrical systems; blowing debris into intakes, skipping a contaminated area, or using an unverified wet chemical creates the hazard the program must control.
stem: A cleaning crew proposes blowing debris into CRAH intakes during work in a live data hall. What should the supervisor require?

choices: Sharing employee badges to save time and bypass logging
No logging of entry
Permanent full access cards for all contractors forever
Scoped vendor access with identity checks and escorts
explanation: Scoped vendor access with identity checks and escorts limits a high-risk path; shared badges, missing logs, or permanent full access defeat accountability and least privilege.
stem: Operational security for vendors performing work includes:

choices: Hiding spare parts offsite without inventory
Disabling monitoring to avoid alarms and notifications
Deleting runbooks to encourage creativity
Procedures, spares, training, labels
explanation: Procedures, spares, training, and labels reduce MTTR by making recovery repeatable; disabling monitoring or deleting runbooks removes the preparation that shortens repair.
stem: Reducing MTTR in facility operations is often less about buying new gear and more about:

choices: Facility changes cannot affect availability when the servers have two cords
A software-change record is sufficient even when facility work is unrecorded
A hallway agreement is sufficient if an experienced technician is present
Without a controlled record and MOP, facility work can become a self-inflicted outage
explanation: The missing record and MOP leave a dual-cord cutover vulnerable to a self-inflicted outage; redundant cords do not remove facility-change risk, and experience or software-only records are not substitutes for controlled work.
stem: A planned dual-cord cutover has no written change record and relies on a hallway agreement. What risk should the review flag?

choices: Use circuit labels mainly to index annual photos and facilities records
Treat consistent label colors as sufficient without circuit, source, and destination identifiers
Use labels for visitor wayfinding while keeping emergency paths in operator memory
Emergency isolation and load migration
explanation: Circuit, source, and destination labels let operators identify paths during isolation and load migration; photo indexing, color alone, or visitor wayfinding does not provide emergency path identity.
stem: Labelling that includes circuit ID, source panel, and destination helps most during:

choices: Maintenance always succeeds on first try
Rollback is never useful in any maintenance change
Abort and restore a known-good state
Monitoring should be off during all maintenance
explanation: Abort criteria and rollback restore a known-good state when maintenance deviates; rollback remains useful, and disabling monitoring removes the evidence needed to decide.
stem: Preventive maintenance windows scheduled without rollback criteria are weak because:

choices: Disturbing dust and opening tiles can alter airflow
Floor cleaning has no effect on cooling, airflow, or contamination
CRAH units can improve when clogged with dust and filters
Containment doors should be removed permanently for cleaning access
explanation: Opening tiles and disturbing dust can alter airflow and contamination; cleaning does affect cooling, and permanently removing containment is not a safe access method.
stem: Cleaning under raised floors and inside perforated tiles should be coordinated with cooling operations because:

choices: Only cosmetic bezels and noncritical appearance parts
Zero inventory to maximize accounting metrics only and accept delays
Random consumer parts with no BOM match or compatibility
Long-lead critical components prevent site stranding
explanation: Critical long-lead spares prevent site stranding; zero inventory or random incompatible parts lengthen MTTR rather than improving readiness.
stem: Spare-parts strategy linked to MTTR targets should prioritize:

choices: Photos have no information value or security impact
Detailed internals can aid attacks if leaked
Project layouts should be posted on social media to document breaker transparency
Cyber teams can care about physical layouts and access rather than operations
explanation: Detailed layouts can reveal physical attack paths; treating photos as harmless or posting them as transparency exposes information, and physical layout is relevant to security as well as cyber operations.
stem: Security-aware operations include controlling photographs and publicly posted rack layouts because:

choices: Never, once the first PDF is printed
Update when the field changes
Only when an auditor is parking outside
By memory during the next outage
explanation: Update controlled drawings when the field changes; waiting for an auditor or relying on memory during an outage leaves operators with a trusted-wrong path.
stem: Documented single lines, rack elevations, and cable schedules should be updated:

choices: A four-hour response commitment obliges the vendor to stock spares for covered equipment
Holding critical spares on site would void the equipment manufacturers warranty
Mean time to repair has a statutory definition that overrides the contract
Response time can differ from restore time
explanation: An SLA that commits to a response clock says when someone arrives, not when service returns -- the two are separate measures and only the second is what the business experiences. That is why a four-hour response can sit in front of a multi-day outage when the part is not on the shelf. The tempting reading is that a response commitment implies a spares commitment; it does not, which is exactly the gap the question is about, and stocking spares locally is a normal practice rather than a warranty risk. Repair-time definitions are contractual terms too, negotiated between the parties rather than fixed by statute.
stem: An SLA that promises four-hour onsite response but stocks no critical spares may still yield long outages because:

choices: Replace the need for unique circuit IDs
Allow deleting panel schedules
Reduce cognitive load and misinterpretation when multiple teams and shifts work the plant
Are purely decorative with no ops effect
explanation: Standard visual language reduces misinterpretation under stress but does not replace unique circuit IDs, panel schedules, or the operational meaning of labels.
stem: Color-coding and standardized label templates across a campus help because they:

choices: LOTO where applicable, PPE, training, and respect for energized boundaries—not heroics
Working alone on unfamiliar switchgear without briefing
Using water freely on electrical faults
Disabling safety interlocks for speed
explanation: LOTO, PPE, training and defined energized-work boundaries are the controls; working alone on unfamiliar gear, using water near an electrical fault, or defeating an interlock each remove a control rather than supply one. Mind the boundary between the two standards: 1910.147 governs hazardous-energy control generally and does not cover work on electric utilization equipment such as switchgear, which falls under Subpart S -- so the electrical safe-work-practice authority is 1910.333, not 147.
stem: Operational safety near live electrical and mechanical plant requires:

choices: The exam-weight section of the public 2.1 heading — invent a percentage so the brochure can be scored
The service catalog is the CMMS asset register, so owner, SLO, OLA, and underpinning contract pointers are unnecessary
Sufficient if sales published it this quarter and the logos are current

A brochure, not a catalog. The catalog is the owned list of delivered services (SKU, owner, SLO pointer, OLA or UC underneath); a 40 kW liquid SKU sitting on a 10 kW air-hall OLA is how the org-split starts
explanation: A catalog without owners is a brochure. Each entry names the service, who provides it, the SLO it points at, and the OLA or UC that makes that SLO possible. Do not invent an exam-weight percentage for this heading.
stem: A slide of logos titled “service catalog,” with no SKU, no owner, no SLO pointer, and no OLA or underpinning contract underneath, is:

choices: Treat the vendor clause as an OLA because any written SLA commitment is an internal customer instrument and UC term
Approve: four-hour onsite response is the customer SLA, and SLM invents its own nines table

Reject the packet: SLA is the customer instrument, OLA is internal team-to-team, UC is the vendor — four-hour onsite response is a UC term, not the tenant SLA; three documents that cannot add up are not SLM; availability clocks stay as in Module 01, not a new nines table
Collapse OLA and underpinning contract into one synonym so the stack has fewer documents
explanation: Analyze the stack collapse. SLA, OLA, and UC have different counterparties. A vendor response-time clause is not the customer SLA. SLM does not invent a nines table. No invented outage percent.
stem: Reviewer is handed an SLM packet: “Tenant restore-in-four-hours is the SLA; the NOC pages facilities when we can; the vendor clock starts when the part ships; the maintenance agreement’s four-hour onsite response IS the customer SLA; write a new nines table so SLM can own availability.” You should:

choices: Org structure is an exam-weight percentage, so the staffed path and reporting line do not matter

Functions (facilities, NOC/ops, security, EHS, floor, vendor management) must have a path: NOC is not isolation authority on switchgear (Subpart S), and a Safety Officer reporting to the uptime bonus is a fictional independent veto
Module 01 already named four functions and seats, so the organizational-structure heading is empty and this file should repeat them
The NOC should own Subpart S isolation because it holds the DCIM screen
explanation: Name the functions and the split. Isolation authority is not a NOC screen. A Safety Officer under the uptime bonus is not an independent veto. Do not grow this back into Module 01’s four-seat lesson. Do not invent an exam-weight percentage.
stem: This file owns the 2.1 organizational-structure heading — the staffed path, not Module 01’s four seats. A site that leaves switchgear isolation with the NOC alone, and parks the Safety Officer under the manager whose bonus is uptime, is failing that heading because:

choices: Enough training produces infallible night-shift operators, so the matrix is optional once the class is complete
A signed attendance sheet plus an EPI / certification hour-count substitutes for competence records
Vendor classes are forbidden and only in-house authors may teach

The programme is a role-based matrix with initial qualification, a named recurrent interval, procedure-change training, drills, and competence records — and DOE-HDBK-1028 still holds: no amount of training alters fallibility
explanation: Training is a role-based control with competence records, not a vendor-class receipt: an attendance sheet or EPI hour-count proves presence, not ability, and vendor instruction is not forbidden. DOE-HDBK-1028 still holds that training does not remove human fallibility.
stem: A site whose training programme is “we sent people to a vendor class” is missing the 2.1 control because:

choices: Least privilege if the contractor signed an NDA and the visitor book has a name
The Module 13 role × zone × privilege diagram copied onto a card
A security matrix with one convenient row, so the printer can stay simple

Not a matrix. A matrix is role × zone × privilege (unescorted, escorted-only, no-access, time-window, two-person); a badge that opens every zone is a single failure that looks like convenience. Module 13 owns the layers; this file owns the table
explanation: A security matrix maps role, zone, and privilege; an NDA, a copied diagram, or one all-zone badge does not enforce least privilege. Physical layers stay in Module 13.
stem: A contractor badge programmed to open lobby, grey space, white space, UPS room, and BESS yard, unescorted, at any hour, is:

choices: A document, not a procedure. Level of use is the attribute that decides whether the paper is open at the step or read beforehand and worked from memory; a programme must specify use requirements
Valid as long as the author was also the sole validator
Automatically emergency-response use, so the reader may skip the steps
Still a procedure if the approval signatures are wet-ink and the font of the warnings is large
explanation: DOE O 422.1 requires a declared procedure-use level; sole-author validation, an assumed emergency shortcut, or wet signatures cannot replace the use requirement that keeps the worker at the step.
stem: A MOP whose cover block never names use-each-time versus reference use is, per DOE O 422.1:

choices: Subpart S applies only to the utility’s exclusive-control substation — that regime is 1910.269, not this work

1910.147(a)(1)(ii)(D) excludes electrical-hazard exposure on electric-utilization installations and points to Subpart S (1910.331–.335, principally 1910.333). Putting a UPS into maintenance bypass from its HMI is not isolation — physical disconnect, lock, stored energy released, absence of voltage verified including backfeed
The only applicable rule is the utility’s own tariff, because the campus takes a medium-voltage feed
1910.147 already covers every electric-utilization installation, so a second citation is decoration
explanation: Subpart S covers electrical-hazard work on utilization installations, and HMI bypass or a utility tariff does not provide physical isolation; 1910.147 alone is not a blanket substitute for disconnecting, locking, releasing, and verifying absence of voltage.
stem: An energy-control programme that cites only 29 CFR 1910.147 for work on UPS, switchgear, PDU, and busway is mis-scoped because:

choices: A BMS/DCIM point proves the floor is healthy whenever the point stays silent — absence of alarm is health
A reason to raise the integrator’s invoice until every status bit is an alarm

A status indicator, not an alarm. HSE: process status indicators should not be designated as alarms; delete or downgrade, do not acknowledge forever. Point count and operator-actionable alarms per hour move in opposite directions
A high-priority alarm so it is never missed, and more points always mean better monitoring
explanation: HSE's alarm-handling guidance distinguishes an alarm that requires operator action from a process-status indication, and sets priority by the consequence of failing to respond. The official 2003 blackout report supplies the bounded failure lesson that a silent alarm path is not evidence of system health. Point count is not a substitute for an actionable response design; no universal alarm threshold or outage percentage is inferred.
stem: A BMS/DCIM point with no defined operator response, and a procurement that prices the job by monitored-point count, should be read as:

choices: Refuse: floor management is work control on the live floor — who is on the floor, the PTW board, and the heat/power/liquid budget of the change — not a synonym for cleaning. Two MOPs on one loop and an uncounted N+1 are the heading failing
Convert the missing N+1 into an invented outage percentage so the packet can be scored
Approve: cleaning is the 2.1 heading, so the rota is the programme; simultaneous MOPs on one CDU loop, an unlisted vendor, and the N+1 count are housekeeping details
Send everyone to an EPI / certification class; a credential hour-count substitutes for the PTW board
explanation: Floor management controls who is present, live work, permits, and remaining capacity; a cleaning rota, an invented outage percentage, or an EPI hour-count does not replace the PTW board and N+1 check.
stem: A change-window packet treats “floor management” as the weekly cleaning rota, while two MOPs share one CDU loop, the PTW board does not list the vendor already in row 12, and nobody has counted whether isolating the CDU spends the remaining N+1. The taught reading is:

choices: Skip review and approve because the author of the new as-built already validated their own work
Treat the share-drive PDF as issued because it is the newest filename
Leave both live until the annual catch-up; two revs are extra assurance

Supersede: mark and pull the old rev from the point of use. Two live revs is the trusted-wrong case — a drawing that shows a disconnect where none exists makes you act. Archive is retention with a retrieval path, not fourteen unmarked copies
explanation: The six-step document-management lifecycle is create, review, approve, issue, supersede, archive. The change that altered the plant issues the new as-built; the previous rev is marked and pulled. Annual catch-up is not a step. No invented outage percent.
stem: Close-out of a live-plant change issues a new as-built. The previous revision is still unmarked in the UPS-room binder and as a share-drive PDF titled “final.” The document-management decision is:

choices: Accept the SLA filing: any written response time is an operational level agreement, and the vendor is an internal team
The operational level agreement is the customer SLA credit schedule under another name, so the vendor four-hour clause is the SLA
Collapse the operational level agreement into the SLA and invent a new nines table so SLM owns availability

The operational level agreement is an internal team-to-team hand-off (facilities ↔ NOC ↔ security ↔ floor) that makes the customer SLA possible; the vendor clause is an underpinning contract, not the operational level agreement and not the tenant SLA
explanation: Spell it: operational level agreement is internal. SLA is the customer instrument. UC is the vendor. A four-hour onsite response is a UC term. SLM does not invent a nines table. Contributing factors stay plural. No invented outage percent.
stem: A tenant restore-in-four-hours SLA is said to be “covered” by a vendor four-hour onsite-response clause that someone filed as the operational level agreement. The distinction is:

choices: Nothing is missing — the STOPPED display confirms the fan is not turning, so the equipment is safely deenergized for work
Lockout device application — the padlock is on the HMI door rather than the panel door, so a second signature is required
Nothing is missing for mechanical work — the sequence would only fail if the CRAH shared a chilled-water header with the adjacent unit
Isolation — a control-circuit device is not an energy isolating device, so nothing physically preventing energy transmission was operated
explanation: 1910.147(b) defines an energy isolating device as a mechanical device that physically prevents transmission or release of energy — a breaker, disconnect switch, line valve, block — and states plainly that push buttons, selector switches and other control-circuit type devices are NOT energy isolating devices. 1910.333(b)(2)(ii)(B) reinforces it: control-circuit devices such as push buttons, selector switches and interlocks may not be used as the sole means for deenergizing, and interlocks may not substitute for lockout and tagging. The HMI reports the control state, not the energy state — the supply conductors remain connected. The (d)(1)-(6) sequence therefore stalls at isolation, before lockout application, stored-energy release, and verification. Locking a control enclosure locks the control. The upstream distribution type does not change the definition.
stem: A CRAH is to be worked on. The technician selects the unit's HMI "maintenance mode", which opens the fan contactor and shows STOPPED, padlocks the HMI enclosure, and signs the permit. Which step of the energy-control procedure has not actually been performed?

choices: Orderly transfer of the lockout device to the oncoming technician, so the isolation is never left unheld at any point
Removal of the off-going lock at end of shift and application of a fresh lock when the oncoming technician takes over
Reassignment of the permit to the oncoming shift supervisor, whose signature carries the isolation until the crew returns
A tag on the device naming the off-going technician and a contact number, since a tag documents isolation when no one is on site
explanation: 29 CFR 1910.147(f)(4) requires an orderly transfer of lockout devices at shift change so protection is continuous; removing the outgoing lock before the incoming lock is applied leaves the isolation unheld, while a signature or tag documents the handover but does not hold the isolation. The on-site and vendor employers must also share their energy-control procedures under (f)(2), and stored energy must remain verified under (d)(5)(ii).
stem: A vendor crew has a chilled-water pump locked out and the job will run past shift change. The off-going technician's personal lock is the only lock on the isolating device. What must the energy-control procedure require at the handover?

choices: The contractor's own supervisor signs the job sheet, since the contractor performed the work and is closest to its condition
The shift engineer gives a verbal all-clear on the bridge once the contractor confirms the actuator is operating correctly
The escort countersigns the visitor log on leaving, which closes the work and releases the plant back to operations
The permit originator declares the equipment ready for normal use, so return to service is authorised by the permit
explanation: Before return to service, the permit originator must declare the equipment ready for normal use; finishing the job, an escort's visitor record, or the contractor's own completion does not authorize plant hand-back, and a verbal all-clear leaves no documented declaration. HSE permits-to-work guidance supports this separation.
stem: A contractor has finished replacing a valve actuator on a chilled-water branch. The work is done, the area is tidy and the escort is ready to sign the visitor log. Under a permit-to-work system, what has to happen before that branch is returned to normal service?

choices: A declaration from those involved in the handover, so the permit carries the change of authorising and working parties
An extension signed by the oncoming supervisor, since the work is unchanged and only the time window needs to move
A verbal briefing at the shift meeting covering every open job, which is what the operations handover log exists to capture
Re-issue of a fresh permit to the oncoming parties, because the original permit lapses with the shift that raised it
explanation: At shift change, the people authorizing and carrying out the work must declare the handover on the existing permit; a verbal briefing or general log leaves the permit unchanged, a fresh permit breaks continuity, and an extension changes duration rather than parties. HSE permits-to-work guidance supports this boundary.
stem: A live permit for work inside a switchroom will still be open when the shift changes at 19:00. Both the issuing authority and the working party will be relieved by their oncoming counterparts. What does the permit system require at that boundary?

choices: The matrix is complete — sensor, setpoint and priority are the three required columns for operational sign-off
Add owner and next action — without a named responder and defined response, the matrix cannot drive operations
Add a point-count column so future procurement can be priced by total sensor quantity across the floor
Delete priority since all alarms on a critical floor carry equal weight and require the same response time
explanation: HSE's 'Better alarm handling' gives the design rule: an alarm requires operator action, and priority is set by the consequence of the operator failing to respond. A matrix that lists sensors and setpoints but omits who responds and what they do cannot be used operationally — the midnight call reaches a point name, not a person or a procedure. Adding point-count inverts the metric: alarm quality is measured in operator-actionable alarms per hour, not sensor quantity, and the two move in opposite directions.
stem: A BMS vendor delivers a 'facilities monitoring matrix' that lists sensor tag, setpoint, and alarm priority. What gap should the review catch before sign-off?

choices: Page operations — one unit lost means escalate now, because the next failure is an outage with no warning
Wait for the BMS to confirm the trip for ten minutes before escalating, to filter nuisance pages from real events
Page only if the remaining chiller shows a warning alarm, since a healthy standby unit needs no attention
No page — cooling is still available, so the redundancy-loss event is informational only and needs no escalation
explanation: The 2003 blackout report names the failure mode: 'absence of alarm was read as evidence of health' while the alarm system itself was down. The counter-rule is to escalate when redundancy is lost, not when the service fails. A single-chiller plant with no fault indication is still a single point of failure — the next trip is an outage. Waiting for a warning alarm or a confirmation window delays the page past the point where intervention can restore redundancy before the second failure.
stem: A notification matrix says 'page on loss of redundancy' for the chiller plant. One of two chillers trips; the floor stays cool. What should the escalation path do?

choices: Keep the role-based training matrix because the vendor sent a change notice
Update role training before the changed duty begins
Wait for an incident, then train only the person who changed it
Replace the matrix with one annual attendance total
explanation: Role-based training must be updated before the changed control-system duty begins; a vendor notice is not the affected role's training record, and waiting for an incident reverses the control's timing. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-3 and AT-3(1) cover changed duties and environmental controls.
stem: The skills matrix for a data-center facilities team lists HVAC, power, and fire-detection roles. A control-system change is approved, but no role-based training update is planned. What manager action is directly supported?

choices: Leave the vendor badge active because a signed contract is the access authorization
Remove the vendor from the access list when access is no longer required
Keep the badge active until the next quarterly security review
Move the badge to a shared visitor account so the audit trail stays short
explanation: Remove a vendor from the authorized-access list when the contract need ends; a signed contract is not a continuing badge authorization, and a shared visitor account or quarterly review leaves least privilege stale. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-2 supports the control.
stem: A maintenance vendor's contract ended Friday, but its badge still appears on the facility access list Monday. What control action should the CDFOM manager take?

choices: Plan environmental-support capacity for the contingency
Add a service-catalogue label for the cooling loop
Add a second vendor invoice to the asset register
Add a badge review for alternate-site visitors during contingency
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-2 requires contingency requirements for essential functions, recovery objectives and priorities, roles, and continuity. CP-2(2) adds capacity planning so necessary information-processing, telecommunications, and environmental-support capacity exists during contingency operations. An alternate-site label or badge review does not test whether the degraded cooling service can support the mission.
stem: A BIA says a primary cooling loop can be lost during a contingency. The draft plan lists an alternate site and an RTO but no degraded-capacity check. What management gap remains?

choices: Open a purchase order even when the controller is repaired
Close the controller record when the vendor returns it after removal approval
Delete the old record when the replacement arrives
Add removal approval and a post-repair control check
explanation: Off-site repair needs removal approval and a post-repair control check; a work order or replacement purchase record does not verify that the affected controls still function. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MA-2 requires both controls.
stem: A controller is sent off-site for repair. The maintenance record has a work order, but no approval for removal and no post-repair control check. Which CDFOM review finding is supported?

choices: Add a rack elevation for the replacement module
Document a process for supply-chain weaknesses
Add a customer survey of the module's appearance
Add a warranty extension instead of a risk review
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-3 requires a process to identify and address weaknesses or deficiencies, selected controls to protect against supply-chain risks, and documentation of those processes and controls. Its discussion expressly spans acquisition, delivery, integration, operations, maintenance, and disposal. The control is a lifecycle risk process, not a rack drawing, appearance survey, or warranty substitute.
stem: A replacement power module comes from a single supplier. The lifecycle review reaches disposal but has no documented process for supply-chain weaknesses. What is missing?

choices: Measure only invoice accuracy in the provider review
Document oversight roles and monitor compliance
Use an informal promise from the account lead
Match the provider's uniform to site operations
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 requires external providers to meet defined organizational security and privacy requirements, documents organizational oversight and user roles, and uses ongoing processes to monitor compliance. The discussion also describes service-level agreements as defining measurable outcomes, remedies, and response requirements. Price, uniforms, and an informal promise do not establish that oversight chain.
stem: A monitoring vendor's contract states only a monthly price and response phone number. Which addition is directly supported for an external service?

choices: Inspect annually, correct gaps, and record details
Ask the vendor to approve the employer's internal inspection
Wait for an incident before inspecting the procedure
Replace the inspection with a monthly availability report
explanation: The LOTO procedure needs an annual independent inspection, correction of deviations, and a record of the equipment, date, employees, and inspector; a vendor approval, incident-triggered review, or availability report does not replace that inspection. 29 CFR 1910.147(c)(6) sets the control.
stem: A site's LOTO file has a procedure and training roster, but no record of the annual independent inspection. Which management action is required?

choices: Accept the manuals as a substitute for operator training
Accept startup as proof that every subsystem will interact correctly
Flag missing integrated tests, training, and records
Postpone commissioning until the maintenance contract expires
explanation: Commissioning must verify interactive performance and provide O&M training and records; a contractor startup checklist does not prove subsystem interaction, while postponing commissioning loses the hand-off control. DOE FEMP's 2006 guide supports this boundary.
stem: A new chilled-water plant passes the contractor's startup checklist, but the project file has no integrated functional tests, O&M training record, or final system documentation. What review should flag this?

choices: Delay hand-off until the next maintenance review
Replace succession planning with one exit interview
Trust vendor manuals to transfer all local knowledge
Document knowledge for succeeding staff
explanation: Documented O&M knowledge must pass to succeeding staff; vendor manuals, a single exit interview, or a delayed review do not preserve site-specific operating knowledge. DOE FEMP's 2006 commissioning guide treats training and documentation as hand-off controls.
stem: A commissioning lead leaves before hand-off. The project has no training record or O&M documentation package. What succession risk is directly visible?

choices: Define a secure disposal strategy first
Remove it and review the remaining service later
Treat the vendor invoice as the disposal plan
Send it to recycling before recording the state
explanation: A secure disposal strategy must precede removal so the gateway reaches an acceptable secure state without weakening remaining monitoring; an invoice, later review, or immediate recycling is not a disposal control. NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1 supplies the lifecycle boundary.
stem: A facilities manager retires one control-system gateway while the monitoring service remains online. Which asset-management action fits NIST's disposal process?

choices: Keep only a recycler invoice after the hand-off
Record sanitization and its destination
Transfer it after confirming the hardware still boots
Rely on the previous tenant's confidentiality label
explanation: Reuse requires recorded sanitization and destination because a device that boots is not evidence that prior data was removed; a recycler invoice or confidentiality label alone cannot prove sanitization. NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 requires the decision, verification, validation, and records.
stem: A retired storage device will be reused by another tenant. Which manager control best matches NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2?

choices: Let the construction contractor alone review acceptance
Treat operator preparation as optional after startup
Use an independent commissioning provider
Wait for the first maintenance failure to appoint a reviewer
explanation: Total Building Commissioning uses an independent provider to verify interactive performance and prepare operators; the construction contractor alone lacks the required independence, and optional operator preparation or waiting for failure is not commissioning. GSA PBS P100 2024 §1.8.4 supports this arrangement.
stem: A public-building project is selecting its Total Building Commissioning provider. Which arrangement matches GSA PBS P100 2024?

choices: Add a logo index and omit operating availability
Provide a central list of supported services and availability
Replace it with a spare-parts export
Publish a project list without service ownership or availability
explanation: The UK Department for Education's Service Management standard, Version 1, lists Service Catalogue Management among its practices and says the standard provides a central list and availability of supported services. A logo slide, project list, or spare-parts export is not that service view.
stem: A service catalogue for data-centre operations contains logos and project names but no supported-service list or availability view. What correction fits the public service-management standard?

choices: Replace the SLA with a facilities asset register
Treat the phone number as the OLA and stop reviewing performance
Publish an uptime percentage without owners or remedy terms
Define cross-team OLA duties and measurable SLA outcomes
explanation: An external-service arrangement needs defined oversight roles and measurable SLA outcomes; a phone number, asset register, or invented uptime percentage does not establish cross-team OLA duties or provider accountability. NIST SP 800-53 SA-9 supports the oversight boundary.
stem: A facilities provider's SLA names a price and a phone number; internal facilities and NOC commitments are absent. Which review action is supported?

choices: Freeze the process until a new service catalogue is approved
Use trends to identify improvement opportunities
Replace trend review with a one-time satisfaction survey
Count dashboard points and call the largest count the improvement
explanation: Trend analysis should identify improvement opportunities; freezing the process, taking one satisfaction snapshot, or selecting the largest dashboard count does not close the continual-improvement loop. The UK Department for Education Service Management standard supports this practice.
stem: A service-improvement process has a monthly report but no way to turn observed trends into changes. What supported next step is missing?

choices: Wait for an evacuation drill before documenting any of the missing plan steps
Add evacuation, accounting, critical-operations, contact, and review steps
Keep the contact-only plan if the alarm test passes
Move every emergency-plan detail into a vendor SLA and close the gap
explanation: An emergency plan needs evacuation, critical-operations, accountability, contact, and review steps; passing an alarm test or moving detail into a vendor SLA does not supply those response elements. 29 CFR 1910.38(b), (c), and (f) support the finding.
stem: A data-centre emergency plan names a contact but omits evacuation routes, critical operations before evacuation, employee accounting, and review after changes. What finding is supported?

choices: Replace it with a vendor invoice and a maintenance calendar only
Limit it to badge counts because equipment status is an engineering matter
Transfer equipment status, duties, and active or planned work
Add a service-level percentage and leave the turnover record unchanged
explanation: A proper turnover transfers equipment status, duties, and active or planned work; a badge count, vendor invoice, or service percentage does not relieve the incoming operator. NE O 422.1 Attachment 2 paragraph 2.l supports this bounded conduct-of-operations model.
stem: A night-shift turnover says 'all normal' but lists neither equipment status nor in-progress work, and the oncoming operator cannot identify relief duties. What gap does the public conduct-of-operations model expose?

choices: Keep both PDFs active so operators can choose the familiar version
Treat the approval signature as proof that every revision was tested
Control revisions, test the procedure, and issue the current copy
Replace procedure review with the vendor's annual invoice
explanation: NE O 422.1 Attachment 2 paragraph 2.p and Appendix A 2.p.(4),(6)-(9) require processes for procedure changes and approval, initial issue and periodic review/testing, availability and use of the latest revisions, and defined procedure-use requirements. A past approval does not validate an untested revision or authorize two uncontrolled copies.
stem: An MOP was approved once, but its revision was never tested and an obsolete PDF remains at the operator console. What control is missing?

choices: Add a second badge reader while leaving records and keys unchanged
Replace the SOP with a visitor survey and a monthly door count
Keep access logs and change keys on the defined triggers
Trust the badge vendor's firmware report as the facility access record
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 requires verification of individual access authorizations and controlled ingress/egress, maintenance of physical-access audit logs, and changes to combinations or keys at the defined frequency and when keys are lost, compromised, or their holders transfer or terminate. A reader or vendor report does not replace those procedure controls.
stem: A physical-security SOP verifies a badge at entry but never keeps access logs or changes keys when a holder transfers. What gap remains?

choices: Set review timing/events and coordinate findings with response
Add more cameras but leave review timing and escalation undefined
Wait for a second incident before connecting the logs to response
Replace access-log review with a cleaning rota and occupancy estimate
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-6(a)-(c) requires monitoring physical access, reviewing logs at an organization-defined frequency and when defined events or indications occur, and coordinating review and investigation results with incident response. More cameras do not supply the missing review and coordination process.
stem: During a floor review, access logs are examined only after a security incident and the results never reach incident response. Which control gap is clearest?

choices: Add a point-count column and keep response and reporting unspecified
Wait for a failed component before setting any monitoring or reporting frequency
Treat a silent point as evidence that the monitored service is healthy
Define metrics, cadence, assessment, analysis, response, and status reporting
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7(a)-(g) requires a continuous-monitoring strategy with defined metrics, monitoring and assessment frequencies, ongoing assessments and monitoring, correlation and analysis, response actions, and status reporting to defined personnel or roles at a defined frequency. The item applies those control fields to the facilities-matrix artifact named by the CDFOS heading; it does not claim that CA-7 prescribes a particular vendor matrix format.
stem: A facilities monitoring matrix lists points but not monitoring or assessment cadence, correlation, response owner, or reporting frequency. What source-backed gap remains?

choices: Publish only a user quick-start and omit the administrator maintenance detail
Replace system documentation with a vendor invoice and an asset count
Keep the pack local to the author because operators can request it later
Develop and distribute administrator and user documentation
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-5(a) requires administrator documentation for secure configuration, installation, operation, maintenance, and known vulnerabilities. SA-5(b) covers user functions, secure interaction, and user responsibilities; SA-5(c) addresses unavailable documentation; and SA-5(d) requires distribution to defined personnel or roles. This item does not assert the six undocumented sub-processes from the CDFOS syllabus.
stem: An operations documentation pack has no administrator instructions for secure operation or maintenance, no user responsibilities, and no distribution list. What action is supported?

choices: Keep a maintenance record and terminate the session when work ends
Accept it because approval and strong authentication remove the record need
Replace the report with a purchase order and leave the connection available
Require a marketing summary before the next maintenance window
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MA-4(a)-(e) requires approval and monitoring of nonlocal maintenance, policy-consistent tools, strong authentication, records of the activity, and termination of the session and network connections when maintenance is complete. Approval and authentication are complementary controls, not substitutes for the service report or close-out.
stem: A remote maintenance vendor was approved and authenticated, but the service report has no session record and the connection stayed open after the work. Which finding is supported?

choices: Use job-based IDPs with competency goals
Reserve career development for employees after promotion
Use one annual attendance total detached from job duties
Treat a vendor completion badge as the succession plan
explanation: A job-based IDP with competency goals is the grounded manager artifact: the current public OPM career-development guidance describes IDPs as records of career goals, development objectives, and training opportunities such as rotational assignments, and ties them to learning objectives and competencies. This is a curriculum grounding receipt, not a credential or certification claim.
stem: A DOE facilities department is planning development for shift leads. Which manager artifact matches DOE O 360.1D?

choices: Let each plan owner exercise alone
Name an alternate site and skip joint exercises
Test, review, and correct
Wait for an outage before testing the plan
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4(a)-(c) requires testing the contingency plan at an organization-defined frequency, reviewing test results, and initiating corrective actions when needed. CP-4(1) adds coordination with organizational elements responsible for related plans, including business-continuity and emergency-related plans. The control does not prescribe a numeric cadence here.
stem: A BIA-backed business-continuity plan is never exercised; results are not reviewed, and related plans are tested separately. What manager action is supported?

choices: List the site in the BIA without readiness checks
Treat primary-site controls as proof for the alternate
Rely on the contract until a transfer begins
Prepare the alternate site with resources
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-7(a)-(c) requires arrangements for transfer and resumption, equipment and supplies or contracts supporting delivery, and controls equivalent to those at the primary site. CP-7(4) requires preparing the alternate site so it can serve as the operational site, including consistent configuration settings and essential supplies and logistics. A contract or BIA entry alone is not readiness evidence.
stem: A selected alternate site has a contract but no equipment, supplies, or equivalent controls prepared. What resilience gap remains?

choices: Wait for a failure before reviewing vendor personnel
Let the contract substitute for access authorization and supervision
Authorize personnel and assign supervision
Count badges without naming maintenance supervisors
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MA-5(a)-(c) requires a process for authorizing maintenance personnel and maintaining an authorized list, verification that non-escorted personnel have required access authorizations, and designated organizational personnel with the required authorization and technical competence to supervise when needed. A commercial contract or badge count does not supply those control decisions.
stem: A maintenance vendor has an active contract but no authorized-personnel list, and unescorted technicians have no technically competent site supervisor. What is missing?

choices: Set a post-failure time for support or spares
Treat preventive work as proof a spare is available
Record purchase cost and omit response timing
Wait for failure before choosing a response window
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MA-6 requires obtaining maintenance support or spare parts for organization-defined system components within an organization-defined time period of failure. The control leaves the component set and time period to the organization; it does not justify inventing a numeric service level or treating preventive maintenance as evidence that a spare is available.
stem: A manager labels a cooling valve high risk but never sets the time for obtaining support or spare parts after failure. What finding is supported?

choices: Use a contract checkpoint instead of visitor review
Review only after a formal incident is declared
Set retention, review timing, and anomaly routing
Keep names and let door logs supply all context
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-8(a)-(c) requires maintaining visitor access records for an organization-defined time period, reviewing them at an organization-defined frequency, and reporting anomalies to organization-defined personnel. The discussion identifies records such as names, organizations, identification, entry and departure times, purpose, and host; a visitor register without retention, review, and routing controls is incomplete.
stem: A visitor register has names and departure times, but no retention period, review cadence, or anomaly recipient. What audit finding is supported?

choices: Add a logo to the roster and leave authority implicit
Replace the role map with a vendor contact list
Define safety roles, authority, and hazard controls
Wait for an incident before assigning responsibilities
explanation: NE O 422.1 Attachment 2 paragraph 2.a.(1) calls for organizational roles, responsibilities, authority, and accountability; 2.a.(3) addresses monitoring and worker accountability for safe work; and 2.a.(5) addresses hazard analysis and hazard controls. This item applies that public conduct-of-operations model as a benchmark and does not turn it into a universal data-centre regulation.
stem: A data-centre operations program names a safety lead but never states who has safety authority, who is accountable, or how hazards are controlled. What action matches the public conduct-of-operations model?

choices: Allow any technician to bring tools inside
Review tools and inspect diagnostic media
Use vendor packaging instead of inspection
Keep one approval and skip future reviews
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, MA-3(a)-(b) requires approval, control, monitoring, and organization-defined review of system maintenance tools. MA-3(1) calls for inspecting tools for improper or unauthorized modification, and MA-3(2) calls for checking media containing diagnostic or test programs for malicious code before use. No review interval is invented here.
stem: A facilities maintenance tool is approved once, but there is no review cadence and diagnostic media are used without inspection. What source-backed gap remains?

choices: Authorize entry and record components
Log only visitor totals at the receiving desk
Accept deliveries when the courier is known to staff
Track exits but leave incoming components unrecorded
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, PE-16(a) requires authorization and control of defined types of system components entering and exiting the facility, and PE-16(b) requires records of those components. The discussion notes that delivery areas may need restricted access; it does not prescribe a particular holding-area layout or vendor scorecard.
stem: A receiving area accepts system components into the facility and sends them out with no authorization record. Which control fits?

choices: Use defined incident-reporting channels
Wait until the monthly security report is issued
Send every alert to all staff without an owner
Record only incidents affecting service uptime
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, IR-6(a) requires personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident-response capability within an organization-defined time period, and IR-6(b) requires incident information to reach organization-defined authorities. The item does not invent a universal reporting interval or recipient list.
stem: A security incident report says ‘door problem’ but has no route to the response function or defined authority. What gap is clearest?

choices: List only new hardware until the next audit
Replace the inventory with a procurement forecast
Keep a complete, current component inventory
Track serial numbers only after a failure
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, CM-8(a) requires an inventory that accurately reflects the system, includes all components, has needed tracking granularity, and includes information for component accountability; CM-8(b) requires review and update at an organization-defined frequency. CM-8(1) adds updates during component installation, removal, and system updates. This item stays at asset recording and does not claim ISO 55000 or a complete asset-management lifecycle.
stem: An equipment register lists some rack assets but omits components, accountability, and an update cadence. What source-backed correction fits?

choices: Record status, abnormalities, and round review
Replace tours with a monthly vendor invoice
Wait for an alarm before inspecting work areas
Count the rounds and omit abnormal-condition notes
explanation: NE O 422.1 Attachment 2 paragraph 2.b.(1) addresses prompt notification of facility-status changes and abnormalities; 2.b.(3) addresses equipment awareness through inspections, checks, and tours; and 2.b.(4) addresses round sheets or inspection logs, abnormal-condition response, and periodic supervisory review. This is a walk-around-duty item, not a claim about a universal shift-handover program.
stem: A walk-around sheet records ‘normal’ but has no equipment-status checks, abnormal-condition response, or supervisory review. What action matches the conduct-of-operations model?

choices: Provide worker access to the program and SDS
Use container labels but omit the program location
Store the manual with the vendor and review it monthly
Wait for a new chemical before offering training
explanation: 29 CFR 1910.1200(g)(8) requires required safety data sheets to be readily accessible during each work shift. Paragraph (h)(2)(iii) requires employees to be informed of the location and availability of the written hazard-communication program, hazardous-chemical lists, and safety data sheets; (h)(1) and (h)(3) cover initial/new-hazard information and training content. This is a bounded documentation claim, not a claim that the regulation requires a document titled an OH&S manual.
stem: A safety manual is on a locked drive; workers cannot find the written hazard-communication program or safety data sheets during their shift. What correction is supported?

choices: Expose support needs for decisions
Add ticket categories without reviewing demand
Replace service reporting with a project closeout
Publish a satisfaction score without service context
explanation: The UK Department for Education's Service Management standard, Version 1, says its practices provide visibility and awareness of support requirements to enable better decision making and improved demand management. A ticket count without that operational visibility does not satisfy the bounded reporting claim; the item does not invent a KPI or service-level percentage.
stem: A service report lists ticket totals but gives no visibility into support requirements for demand decisions. What supported improvement fits?

choices: Count survey replies without changing the support route
Provide a single entry point for service support
Keep channels separate and compare logos quarterly
Replace support access with a maintenance inventory
explanation: The UK Department for Education's Service Management standard, Version 1, identifies user satisfaction through a single point of entry into service support. The item applies that specific public statement to the CDFOS customer-satisfaction heading; it does not prescribe a particular portal or satisfaction score.
stem: A support process surveys users but forces them to search across unrelated channels for help. What service-management improvement is supported?

choices: Use a vendor talk without an employer record
Wait for an injury before reviewing the program
Certify the assessment and verify PPE training
Keep the briefing and skip written assessment
explanation: Under 29 CFR 1910.132(d)(1)-(2), the employer assesses workplace hazards, selects and provides suitable PPE, and keeps a written certification identifying the workplace, certifier, and assessment date. Paragraphs (f)(1)-(3) require training on PPE use and limitations, employee demonstration of understanding and ability, and retraining when changes or deficiencies make prior training obsolete or inadequate. The cited rule is bounded to its OSHA-covered context; it does not create a universal private-sector training interval.
stem: A PPE program review finds no written hazard-assessment certification and no evidence that affected workers can demonstrate proper use. What manager action is supported?

choices: Use a vendor score instead of risk analysis
Assess, document, and update the risk
Freeze the register until the project closes
List more threats without analyzing impact
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, RA-3(a)-(b) calls for identifying threats and vulnerabilities, determining likelihood and magnitude or impact, and integrating organization-level and system-level risk results. RA-3(c)-(e) covers documenting and disseminating results and reviewing them at an organization-defined frequency; RA-3(f) calls for updates at an organization-defined frequency or when relevant changes occur. The source supplies no universal review interval, so the item does not invent one.
stem: A facilities risk register lists threats but has no likelihood/impact analysis, documented review frequency, or change trigger. What action is supported by NIST RA-3?

choices: Keep the induction unchanged after incidents
Refresh awareness on events and cadence
Replace awareness with a badge inventory
Wait for an audit before updating content
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, AT-2(a) requires initial awareness training and organization-defined recurring or event-triggered training. AT-2(c) requires updating content at an organization-defined frequency or when events occur, and AT-2(d) calls for incorporating lessons learned from security incidents or breaches. This is distinct from AT-3 role-based training: the item addresses general awareness, not a job-specific curriculum.
stem: A physical-security induction occurs once; policy changes and incidents never trigger awareness updates. Which action is supported by NIST AT-2?

choices: Keep contingency planning separate from response
Close the record after detection
Wait for another incident before testing
Add lifecycle and lessons-learned feedback
explanation: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, IR-4(a) defines incident handling across preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery. IR-4(b) requires coordination with contingency planning, and IR-4(c) requires using lessons learned to improve incident procedures, training, and testing. The item tests the control's lifecycle and feedback loop without asserting an invented response time or staffing model.
stem: A security incident process detects events but lacks a containment/recovery sequence, contingency coordination, and lessons-learned update. What gap is clearest under NIST IR-4?

choices: Replace the chart with a vendor contact list
Map accountable roles and control responsibilities
Keep titles only because procedures define every duty
Assign all safety decisions to the newest technician
explanation: The chart must show accountability and control ownership; a vendor contact list, titles without assignments, or handing safety to the newest technician does not establish the safe-work path. DOE NE O 422.1 supplies the bounded model.
stem: A data-center organization chart lists job titles but does not show who owns safe-work accountability or hazard controls. What manager correction is source-supported?

choices: Transfer only the access badge and radio
Close all in-progress work before every turnover
Complete turnover with status, duties, and planned work
Leave the missing work for the next weekly meeting
explanation: Under the bounded DOE NE O 422.1 turnover model, shift relief includes equipment and facility status, duties and responsibilities, in-progress and planned work, and relief of the oncoming operator. It is a conduct-of-operations model, not a claim that every private data center is governed by this Order.
stem: The outgoing shift records equipment status but omits planned work and the incoming operator's transferred responsibilities. What shift-management gap remains?

choices: Make the plan available and add required response elements
Keep it private so responders cannot change it
Replace employee accounting with a vendor notification
Review it only after an emergency occurs
explanation: 29 CFR 1910.38 requires a written workplace-available plan when the rule applies, including emergency reporting, evacuation, critical-operations procedures, employee accounting, rescue or medical duties, and responsible contacts. It also requires trained evacuation assistance and review when the plan or responsibilities change. The item is bounded to the OSHA-covered context.
stem: An emergency plan is kept only in a manager's inbox and does not name evacuation assistance or account for employees. Which review finding is supported?

choices: Report it to OSHA within the applicable 24-hour period
Wait for the monthly meeting because the log is sufficient
Report only if the equipment vendor confirms causation
Record it internally and omit external reporting
explanation: 29 CFR 1904.39 requires reporting a qualifying work-related fatality within 8 hours and a qualifying inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours, using an allowed OSHA reporting channel. The item is bounded to the rule's covered employer and event conditions; it does not create a universal incident-reporting rule.
stem: An OSHA-covered employer learns of a qualifying work-related amputation but plans to wait until the monthly safety meeting. What reporting correction is supported?

choices: Use trend analysis to identify improvements
Delete old totals after each monthly meeting
Treat every spike as proof of a failed service
Replace the dashboard with a vendor brochure
explanation: The DfE Service Management standard, Version 1, identifies opportunities for continuous improvement through trend analysis. The item applies that bounded reporting practice to the CDFOM trend-analysis heading without inventing a threshold, cadence, or vendor taxonomy.
stem: A facilities operations dashboard shows recurring support spikes, but the review only archives monthly totals. What monitoring-control improvement is supported?

choices: Replace service reporting with invoice totals
Hide demand patterns until a contract renewal
Report only events that caused an outage
Provide visibility for decisions and demand management
explanation: The DfE Service Management standard, Version 1, states that visibility and awareness of support requirements enable better decision making and improved demand management. The item tests that public standard statement under the exact CDFOM Service reporting heading, without asserting a particular dashboard format.
stem: A service report lists incidents but gives management no view of support requirements or demand. What reporting purpose is missing?

choices: List only assets that failed during the last quarter
Keep availability details only in individual shift notes
Maintain a central catalogue of supported services
Replace service entries with supplier contact cards
explanation: A service catalogue is a central list of supported services and availability; failed assets, shift notes, and supplier contact cards are fragments, not a service view. The DfE Service Management standard, Version 1, supports that distinction.
stem: A facilities service team has equipment names but no central list of supported services or their availability. What catalogue correction fits the cited standard?

choices: Close requests without recording the user's experience
Measure satisfaction only after a major outage
Measure satisfaction and use the results to improve support
Send users to whichever supplier answered last
explanation: Once support has a single entry point, measuring user satisfaction and using the results for improvement tests the management follow-up without inventing a score or survey instrument.
stem: After a single support entry point is introduced, the useful management follow-up is:

choices: PUE is below 1.4
Sustained outage would cause severe business, legal, or safety impact
The building has a raised floor
All racks exceed 10 kW
explanation: Mission-critical status follows the consequences of interruption; a low PUE, a raised floor, or a rack-density threshold is a facility feature or metric, not the business-impact definition.
stem: A payment processor defines a site as mission-critical mainly because:

choices: Five-nines specifies the required utility-feed topology for a facility
Availability and reliability are identical metrics
Reliability is about how often failures occur; availability includes uptime fraction considering repair
Availability typically applies to network links but not power systems
explanation: Reliability concerns failure frequency; availability also accounts for downtime and repair (MTTR) effects.
stem: Which statement is most accurate?

choices: Owns IT gear in cages/cabinets while the provider owns shared hall power/cooling
Must use only provider-owned servers
Cannot use dual-corded equipment
Owns the chillers and generators
explanation: Retail colocation normally leaves the customer responsible for its IT gear while the provider operates shared hall plant; provider-owned servers, customer-owned chillers, and a ban on dual cords describe different arrangements.
stem: In retail colocation, the customer typically:

choices: Over-documenting MOPs
Using LED lighting
One of several contributing factors on a power, cooling, or network object — not a pie slice and not a memorized survey percentage
A third peer root-cause bucket next to power and cooling
explanation: Human and process conditions contribute to failures in a power, cooling, or network path; lighting and MOP paperwork are not the classification, and the factor is not a peer bucket with a made-up survey share.
stem: When a hall outage is written up, human/process during change is treated as:

choices: A blog post comparing PUE
Local electrical and fire codes enforced by the AHJ
A vendor white paper on airflow
An internal runbook preference
explanation: An Authority Having Jurisdiction enforces adopted electrical and fire code; a PUE blog, vendor white paper, or internal runbook becomes guidance or policy rather than code by itself.
stem: Which is generally enforceable as code rather than a voluntary industry standard?

choices: They are identical rating systems
Only ISO rates data centres
TIA-942 Rated concepts and Uptime Institute Tier are separate frameworks; do not treat brand names as interchangeable
ASHRAE issues Tier certificates
explanation: TIA-942 Rated concepts and Uptime Institute Tier are separate frameworks with different owners and processes; ISO, ASHRAE, and a shared brand word do not turn them into one certificate.
stem: The most careful interview answer about TIA-942 and Uptime Tier is:

choices: Paint color of the lobby
Single substation/path geography with no realistic second feed
Having too many conference rooms
Using 19-inch racks
explanation: Dual-utility feasibility depends on genuinely independent upstream paths and workable geography; lobby colour, meeting rooms, and rack format do not create a second utility feed.
stem: Which site factor most directly threatens long-term dual-utility feasibility?

choices: Generator yard, staging, NOC/security ops, and utility intake space
Only decorative suspended ceiling
Hot-aisle posters
Non-metered PDUs
explanation: Operability needs generator and utility-intake space, staging, and NOC/security operations; a decorative ceiling, poster, or unmetered PDU does not provide those supporting facilities.
stem: A white-space design can still fail operationally if the site lacks adequate:

choices: Store diesel fuel
Deliver cold air and/or route cabling beneath the IT floor
Replace the need for UPS beneath the IT floor
Eliminate grounding
explanation: The raised-floor plenum can deliver supply air and route cabling beneath the IT floor; it is not diesel storage, a UPS replacement, or a way to remove grounding.
stem: A raised-floor plenum is often used to:

choices: Only a uniform floor load rating matters when rolling a heavy UPS battery cart
Rolling load (and concentrated load) ratings of the floor system
PUE only
Lux level
explanation: The battery cart imposes rolling and concentrated loads, so both ratings matter; a uniform floor rating, PUE, or lux value alone does not describe the moving point load.
stem: Which loading concept matters when rolling a heavy UPS battery cart across tiles?

choices: Improves global pressure balance in the affected zone
Can short-circuit supply air and starve distant racks
Increases battery autonomy
Can disable the BMS
explanation: An unplanned tile opening leaks pressurized supply air and can starve distant racks; it does not improve pressure globally, increase battery autonomy, or by itself disable the BMS.
stem: Removing floor tiles in a cold-aisle supply design without a plan often:

choices: Reduce the lighting share of facility energy use
Support safe evacuation and life safety when normal power fails
Provide continuous task illumination for rack work during an outage
Satisfy the monthly generator load-test requirement for the site
explanation: Emergency lighting supports safe egress when normal power fails; it is not a substitute for IT task lighting or a generator load-test control.
stem: Emergency/egress lighting is primarily intended to:

choices: Rack → UPS → Utility → Generator
Utility/generator → transfer → UPS → distribution/PDU → rack
CRAH → UPS → Transformer → Lighting only
